en: The Sutra on the Original Causes and Conditions of the Bodhisattva, Volume One,
compiled by Saṃghasena;
translated by the lay follower (upāsaka) Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming, of the Yuezhi people during the Wu dynasty.
If the mind is narrow and inferior, although one may practice much generosity, the recipient is not pure;
thus, the karmic fruit is meager. However, when practicing the giving of gifts, even if the field of merit is impure, [the result is otherwise].
One who can give rise to a vast mind will receive immeasurable karmic retribution.
I have heard that in the past there was a king named Kṣitīśvara, whose nature was violent and cruel, and who delighted in waging wars of conquest.
At that time, there were eighty thousand kings from small kingdoms who, wearing jeweled crowns upon their heads, constantly came to pay court and serve him;
yet that king was foul-mouthed and his conduct lacked goodness, constantly committing illegal acts to invade and oppress the territories of others.

The king had a minister—a great brahmin who practiced pure conduct and was praised by the wise. His speech was gentle, never uttering anything coarse or evil; whatever he undertook, he could accomplish with speed. With a countenance that was upright and majestic, he was revered by the world. There were no among the four Vedas that he did not master thoroughly;
all the sūtras and śāstras possessed by the various brahmins, he had penetrated and understood without exception.
At that time, the prime minister, his years already advanced in age, fell ill and passed away suddenly after not long.
When the king and the people heard of his death, they were all overcome with grief and their longing for him became unbearable.
At that time, the king’s thoughts did not leave him for even a moment, and he spoke these verses to his ministers and subjects:
"How can this great earth, Suddenly be without a ruler?
Like a ship at sea without a master, It drifts hither and thither with the wind."
The one whom I revere has already achieved success in leaving the household life;
his speech is virtuous and gentle, and he is always able to benefit the world.
How could he have passed away so suddenly, causing my heart such distress and anguish?
"It is just like entering a dark chamber without the light of a lamp.
At that time, the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"We only pray that Your Majesty will broaden your mind and not grieve; do not say that there is no one else in the kingdom fit to serve as a minister."
Although this Brahmin had passed away, his son was young, yet intelligent, wise, and of such upright countenance that none in the world could equal him;

his speech was gentle and pleasing to the hearts of all, he practiced patience with a mind always tranquil, and was free from arrogance, pride, or self-importance; he was extensively learned and well-informed, mastering every scripture, benefiting sentient beings like the Brahma King, and was named Virama.
"I only pray that Your Majesty will immediately appoint this man as your minister.
At that time, the king replied,
"If he has a son such as you describe, it is something I have never heard of since ancient times."
The minister spoke again:
"Great King!
This son of a brahmin constantly seeks the True Dharma and remains aloof from false teachings; yet, while he cherishes his own doctrine, he has not yet been able to do so for others."

The king replied: "If you are indeed a man of talent, how could you violate and destroy the family laws of our ancestors? If one abandons their ancestral occupation, they cannot be called a seeker of the True Dharma. Our late father always assisted me in governing the kingdom through the True Dharma, enabling us to remain far removed from all evils. Although we have conducted such governance and administrative affairs, we have never at any time violated or lost the Brahmanical law. If that person is as you describe, he may be summoned."
The ministers, having received the command, immediately dispatched messengers to summon Virama and bring him to the king’s presence.
Upon arrival, he took his seat and sat with composed dignity, speaking these words:
“Great King!
"For what reason do you deign to address me today?
The king replied immediately,
"Do you not know!"

"Alas for my meager merit! Your father, the prime minister, has unfortunately passed away; the great earth mourns and the people are thrown into turmoil. On his account I am grieved, and my heart is bewildered and distressed."
Then, Vīramatī addressed the king, saying:
"It is not only for Your Majesty that there is such separation from those one loves; this is the inherent characteristic of all conditioned phenomena."
Great King, have you not heard this before?
Whether they be devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—whether old or young—none can escape this passing away.
"Great King!
All sentient beings certainly possess it.
Great King!"
Just as the nature of fire is able to burn all things, so too is the dharma of impermanence, which is able to destroy and annihilate all sentient beings.
Does Your Majesty not know?
Old age, sickness, and death can destroy sentient beings, just as a tree with flowers and fruit at a crossroads is constantly shaken by many people.
"Great King!
It is like a swift river that flows constantly without ceasing; the life-span of sentient beings is just like this, Great King!"
Just as the garuḍa bird plunges into the dragon palaces, seizing and devouring the dragons;
or as the lion displays its fierce majesty amidst a herd of deer and wild boars;
so too is the law of death for all sentient beings who wander and circulate within the three realms.
"Great King!

This law of death cannot be escaped by seeking redemption through wealth or by coaxing and consoling with gentle words; nor can it be warded off or driven away by the force of the fourfold army. Such is the fixed nature of this law of death; it is the constant dharma of all sentient beings."
"For this reason, Great King, you should not give rise to sorrow regarding this.
When the king had heard this, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these words to his ministers:
"It is unprecedented! Although this youth is of tender age, he speaks the words of the ancient sages."
At that time, the king spoke to Virama, saying: "Do you not know?
Your father was as protective of me as he would be of his own infant son; therefore, I now feel the weight of his kindness and am overcome with grief and confusion."

"I am now frail, weak, dull-witted, and ignorant; as you have said, I shall never have a share [of the lineage]. If you would now look upon me with compassion and pity, I pray that you first accept the succession and carry on the family business; I shall, with a sincere heart, take refuge for the rest of my life."
At that time, Vīrama immediately thought to himself:
"How shall I now face this sudden encounter? Hearing these words, I do not know what to do, like a weak man attempting to climb a high mountain on foot."
He further thought to himself:
"Now, although I have inherited the governance of the kingdom from my predecessor and have brought great benefit to the people, the pure and wholesome Dharma I practice has been neglected."

"Your Majesty governs the land in accordance with the hearts of the myriad people, yet there must be immeasurable transgressions and calamities, namely punishments, the plundering of others' wealth, and the intimidation of the world; or they are banished or driven out, for one must follow the King in practicing such laws. If you practice the True Dharma (*saddharma*), my goodness will suffer decline;
if I now intentionally practice the wholesome Dharma, it will not accord with the Great King’s holy intentions. If I were to comply with the King’s law, the wholesome Dharma would daily decay."
While he was thinking this, the king spoke again,
saying, "Great Master, what are you contemplating today?
At that time, Virama replied to the king:

"What I am now contemplating is: by what means may I bring benefit to the King’s person and all the people of the kingdom, ensuring they suffer no decline or loss? Furthermore, I reflect upon the merits and faults of the King and his subjects; if one first performs good deeds and later commits evil, such a person cannot be called human."
"Great King!
It is better to speak words of truth even if they cause enmity and hatred than to speak flattering words even if they bring about intimacy and affection."
"It would be better, Great King, to preach the True Dharma and fall into hell than to preach false and deceitful teachings and be born in the heavens."
I have now reflected upon and deliberated this matter.
Great King!
If there is anyone who can contemplate this meaning, you should know that such a person will be able to benefit all sentient beings.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he spoke again:
“Great Master!
If we can practice the Dharma in this way, the wholesome dharmas we cultivate will not be diminished.”

At that time, Virama immediately received the king’s command and succeeded his father in the office of prime minister. Thereafter, he gradually exhorted and transformed both the king and the eighty-four thousand minor kings, leading them to practice the True Dharma.
He also caused all the people within the kingdom to turn away from and abandon evil, becoming free from craving for the five desires.
At that time, the king practiced immeasurable wholesome dharmas without any distinction from Vīrama and others.
Seeing the king thus, Vīrama felt joy in his heart and spoke these words:
"I have now already cultivated and maintained the kingdom, yet my wholesome dharmas have suffered no decline."
He further thought:
"By what causes and conditions should I now exhort all sentient beings so that they may all be established securely in the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

However, the dispositions of sentient beings differ: some desire to hear the Dharma; some crave wealth and goods; some indulge in the five desires; some delight in affectionate speech; some prefer the bustle of crowds and seek the company of many people; some enjoy following the conduct of virtuous persons; and some take pleasure in much attachment, never feeling satisfied.

"I now fortunately possess great wisdom and skillful means, capable of gathering in all sentient beings and establishing them securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I also have further skillful means."
For example, although the rising sun can illuminate the entire world, it cannot provide light for those who are blind;
I am likewise, for although I can preach the unsurpassed path to all sentient beings, I cannot bring benefit to those who lack the eye of wisdom.

I shall now further provide them with clothing and food until they are fully satisfied; once their hearts are filled with joy, I will then preach the Dharma for them so that they may believe and accept it.
At that time, having reflected upon this meaning, Vīrama went to the king’s presence and spoke these words:
“I have now already performed the Dharma-rites for immeasurable sentient beings.”

If one gathers three dharmas—namely, practicing the True Dharma, accumulating wealth, and fulfilling one's aspirations—then all lands will be peaceful and free from enmity; the True Dharma will increase like the waxing moon, and a good reputation will spread throughout the eight directions, above and below.
"I only pray that Your Majesty will allow me to practice the unsurpassed True Dharma.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King was filled with wonder and joy; his hair stood on end, and he said:
"Great Master!"
"Whatever you desire to do, please inform me so that I may give you my instructions.
Virama said, "I now wish to perform a great universal sacrifice; whatever is required for this sacrifice, please provide it for me."

At that time, the Great King established an almsgiving hall in a spacious area outside the city and adorned it. He made this vow: "I pray only that the Great King may use kind words to exhort and guide those who serve as messengers, so that they do not harbor anger or resentment toward me.
Then the Great King and his attendants were all filled with joy and paid respectful homage, providing all necessary food, drink, and requisites.

Immediately, drums were beaten in all directions to proclaim the command: "If there are any sentient beings who require anything—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses, carriages, incense, flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, dwellings, or lamps—let them all gather here; we shall provide for their needs."
He further spoke in verse:
"For the sake of benefiting all the worlds,
I shall provide whatever things are required by sentient beings."
Even when one must relinquish the body, hands, feet, flesh, and blood,
treating them as if they were mere blades of grass or weeds—
at such a time of making offerings, if you should accept them, [you will attain liberation].
Then one should be single-minded, contemplating wholesome dharmas;
having received offerings, one should not be greedily attached to them,
but should instead benefit all beings through wholesome dharmas.
If by my power I were able to enter nirvana quickly,
it would be for the sake of sentient beings who continue to wander through birth and death;
therefore, I remain for a long time and do not take up nirvana.
"Immeasurable sentient beings have fallen into the prison of old age and death;
I wish to pull them out so that they may forever be free from the far-reaching [suffering].

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vīrama provided offerings such that immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings obtained everything they required according to their wishes, and he skillfully spoke the Dharma, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I now disregard my own person out of concern for yours; you have already accepted my offerings.

You should diligently seek your own benefit by contemplating the True Dharma. When the time of death arrives, though one has parents, wives, children, kinsmen, and immeasurable wealth and treasures, none of these can cause life to endure for even a single moment. When one's life is exhausted, one goes alone to the next world."
"Neither parents, nor wife and children, nor kinsmen, nor wealth and treasures follow one after death; only one's own karma cannot be abandoned.
He then spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"For the sake of parents and kinsmen, One practices unwholesome dharmas."
When life ends and one falls into the three realms of existence, there is no one who follows along.
In this present world, when one undergoes suffering and affliction,
even though there be parents and brothers, they cannot take even a small portion [of that pain].
"How much more so in future ages, when there will surely be those who take one's place;
therefore, you should be single-minded and must not commit evil for the sake of others.
"Venerable sirs!"

Your bodies are now peaceful and free from affliction; that is to say, you are already free from such ailments as old age, pulmonary disease, coughing fits, and headaches. You should therefore diligently practice all wholesome dharmas.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vīrama gathered in sentient beings through the two methods of attraction— namely, material gifts and the Dharma—
and for ninety full days after the summer retreat had concluded, he offered them as a gift of merit.

That is to say: there were eighty thousand golden plates filled with silver grain; eighty thousand silver plates filled with golden grain; eighty thousand young bulls and eighty thousand milch cows, each accompanied by a single calf. Each of these cows yielded one *sheng* of milk daily. Their bodies were wrapped and covered with pure white cotton cloth, and they were adorned and embellished with golden horns and silver hooves.

There were eighty thousand young maidens of upright and beautiful form, adorned with necklaces of gold and jewels. Each woman had a personal attendant to serve her every command, ensuring they remained perfectly clean. Each of these women had a couch made either of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, ivory, or fragrant wood, upon which various rugs and cushions were spread.
There were eighty thousand ox-carts and eighty thousand elephants and horses, as well as various granaries and treasuries containing incalculable amounts of money, wealth, and rare jewels.
Having thus fully adorned these objects, he thought to himself:
"I wonder if there is not even a small amount left of these items for giving.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these words to the brahmins:

"You should know this: I have now gathered such various kinds of gold, silver, women, vehicles, elephants, horses, granaries, and precious treasures solely for your sake. It would be well if you would remain silent and quiet for a short while and listen to my request; thereafter, you may divide them as you please and depart."
At that time, all the brahmins were silent and made no sound.
Then, for the sake of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva admonished his own mind:
"Your mind always seeks karmic rewards for its actions, just like a monkey entering a dense forest."
And he spoke in verse:
"The gift that I now bestow Is for the sake of all sentient beings;
Such a gift as this Truly does not hope for its reward."
May I bestow everything upon all sentient beings, so that they may equally experience happiness;
because you craved virtue, you have long remained in the heavens,
and because you craved evil, you have long dwelt in hell.
Furthermore, due to attachment and craving, one may become such a great donor,
or a poor person; one may practice great giving,
or at times, being self-indulgent, guard wealth with stinginess and greed.
Some, due to their own arrogance, cast themselves into poverty and suffering;
others, through heedlessness, remain long within saṃsāra,
revolving without end, just like a wheel turning upon the earth.
For a long time past, I have followed and served you with reverence;
yet though I have performed such deeds, I have been unable to bring you joy.
May you now abide securely in the unmoving state of tranquility.
"What I now give in alms is entirely for the sake of all sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramati took hold of a ritual pitcher with his right hand; having cultivated his mind with great compassion and out of pity for all sentient beings, he wept and shed tears as he thought:
"What I now bestow is not for the sake of Brahmā, Maheśvara, or Śakra-devendra; even if there were anyone superior to these three, I would still have no desire for it."
Seeking only the Buddha-way, I desire to benefit sentient beings and sever all afflictions.
I shall now relinquish my own body, wife, children, slaves, servants, precious jewels, and dwellings; I seek only liberation and do not seek birth-and-death.
By this gift of a soft woman that I now bestow, may all sentient beings, in future ages, completely sever all craving;
by this gift of the five kinds of cow-products that I now bestow, may all sentient beings, in future ages, always be able to bestow the flavor of the Dharma upon others;
by this gift of such bedding as I now bestow, may all sentient beings, in future ages, all attain the adamantine seat of the Tathāgata.
"I now offer these various kinds of precious jewels; may all sentient beings, in future ages, fully obtain the seven jewels of enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
Having spoken these words, he proceeded from the seat of the senior monk to pour the ritual water for washing, but the water would not flow down, just as a miserly person is unwilling to give alms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had this thought:
"For what reason does this bathing water not flow down?
He then further thought:
“Is it not my wish that it shall not be fulfilled in a future age?
Who has obstructed it so that the water does not flow down? Is it perhaps because there is no one of great virtue here, and others are thus unworthy to receive my offerings?”
"Is it that my giving has not been universal?
Or is it that my servants and attendants are not joyful?
Could it be that there is the taking of life among these people?"
I now know for certain that I am not distressing sentient beings; this gift I now bestow is also a timely gift, and I do not examine whether this recipient is worthy or unworthy.
Yet for what reason does this poured water not descend?
At that time, the Bodhisattva saw that the brahmin had conceived feelings of greed and jealousy toward these women, giving rise to resentment as they each said:
"That woman is beautiful; I should take her, you should not take her."
"That ox is fat and strong; I should take it, you should not.
This applied equally to the golden and silver platters of grain, up to and including precious jewels.
At that time, the Bodhisattva saw the various brahmins greedily contending for objects and harboring mutual anger; he then spoke these words:

"These recipients, with their greedy desires, anger, ignorance, and distracted minds, are unable to receive [this gift]. Such an offering is like a chariot whose axle has broken and whose spokes and rim are shattered, incapable of carrying a load; I, too, am just like this."

The seeds were wholesome, yet the field was poor and barren; because of this recipient, whose mind was not virtuous, this bath-water was unwilling to flow away. Although I have now made such a gift, there was no one to instruct me to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; rather, it was for the sake of all sentient beings that I myself resolved upon this mind.
"Now I shall test myself: if I am truly able to have compassion for sentient beings, let the water flow down.
He then took the jar with his left hand and poured it; the water immediately flowed down into the Bodhisattva’s right hand.

When the brahmins saw this, each felt shame and remorse; they set aside the objects of their offerings and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The brahmins then together prostrated themselves and entreated the Bodhisattva to serve as their preceptor (*upādhyāya*).

The Bodhisattva, out of compassion, accepted them and instructed them to practice and study the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). By these causes and conditions, at the end of their lives they were immediately reborn in the Brahma Heaven, and they caused immeasurable sentient beings to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, they do not perceive "this is a field of merit" or "this is not a field of merit," nor do they discriminate between those who are many friends or few doubters.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices giving—whether the gift be much or little, or good or poor—they should offer it with a single-minded purity, never conceiving a sense of inferiority toward the recipient.
All bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
relinquish their own bodies and lives as if they were mere grass, dung,
or filth. As I have heard:
In the past, there was a king named Sarvadatta.
From the moment of his birth, he spoke these words to his parents:
"Regarding all immeasurable sentient beings, I am able to relinquish even my own cherished body and life, let alone other external things such as precious jewels."
Therefore, his parents respected and esteemed him, and gave him a name, calling him Sarvamdada (Giver of All).
From the moment of his birth, his body and his practice of giving grew together, like the moon from its first appearance until the fifteenth day.

Not long thereafter, his father the King passed away. He immediately succeeded to the great enterprise and ruled the land with hegemony; he transformed the people according to the Dharma and did not oppress the myriad subjects. He protected himself and did not involve himself in the affairs of others, never invading or encroaching upon neighboring kingdoms.

If a neighboring country should come to punish him as before, he is rarely able to capture them; he protects the poor and destitute by providing them with wealth, and he shows reverence to śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

Always with clean hands, he gives food to sentient beings; his mouth constantly proclaims, "I give clothing to this person, I give food to this person, and I give wealth and treasures to this person," while lovingly protecting and looking after them.

At that time, as the Bodhisattva constantly practiced such virtuous giving, the people of neighboring countries heard of the King’s merit and all came to submit to his rule. His territory became so densely populated that there was not a single empty space between them, like a torrential flood on a mountain peak flowing down into ditches, pits, and deep ravines;
or like the tide of the ocean rising during the waxing moon, the foreign subjects who came to submit to his rule filled and crowded the land in just the same way.
The other neighboring countries gradually lost their populations and each gave rise to resentment; they immediately held a council together, resolving that they should go forth to punish [the king].
Having made this deliberation, they promptly arrayed their fourfold army and marched toward his kingdom.
At that time, the frontier guards came from afar to inform the king:
"The hostile enemies of the neighboring kingdom have now pressed upon us, like a violent wind, dark clouds, and a torrential rain."
The king then addressed them, saying:
"You should not disturb my mind.
He then spoke this verse:
"The reason why the neighboring kingdom has come to wage war against our country is solely for the sake of its people and the treasures stored in our treasuries;
how joyful and excellent it is that we shall bestow these upon them!"
I shall renounce them and leave the household life to study the Way.
There are many lands where, for the sake of the five desires,
people encroach upon and seize from others, amassing wealth without satiety.
"You should know that after this king's life has ended,
he will immediately fall into hell, the realm of animals, or the realm of hungry ghosts. Therefore,
I am now unable to harm sentient beings for my own sake, nor can I seize the property of others to save myself."
At that time, the great ministers and the people each spoke these words:
"We pray only this, Great King:

do not depart at once! We ourselves shall be able to confront this enemy; Your Majesty, please wait and observe us. Today we shall strike down these rebels with the five types of weapons—halberds, spears, swords, and lances—just as a violent wind blows apart a mass of rain clouds."
The King then replied:
"Alas, you ministers!
I have known this for a long time; you have conceived great affection, protection, respect, and reverence toward me."
I am well aware that you all are foremost in valor, invincibility, heroism, martial strategy, and counsel.
However, the reason that enemy king has now launched this enterprise is not at all for your sake; it is solely for my own.
Even if he were to come and not harm you, how could you give rise to such an evil thought?
I have known this for a long time: this body of the five aggregates of clinging is like a cluster of arrows; do you not know this?

I have long been telling you, O Minister, that all Bodhisattvas should regard all sentient beings as their only child. You must not give rise to thoughts of anger or malice toward other beings; you should know with certainty that such actions lead to rebirth in hell. Therefore, you ought to cultivate goodness with a single-minded focus.
As these words were being spoken, the bandits arrived and raised a loud, piercing cry.
Upon hearing the sound, the king immediately asked his ministers,
"What is this noise?"
The various ministers and officials, each harboring feelings of grief and sorrow, raised their voices in lamentation and all spoke thus:

"This wicked rebel is innocent of no crime, yet he has caused great harm to the people. He is like a malignant hailstorm that destroys the five grains; like a fierce fire that consumes dry grass; like a violent wind that uproots great trees; and like a lion that slaughters various birds and beasts. The slaughter by this vengeful rebel is just like these."
At that time, the ministers did not obey the king’s command; they immediately dispersed and, having arrayed their fourfold army, went out to engage him in battle.
Lacking a commanding general, the army soon retreated in disarray, and the number of soldiers who lost their lives was beyond calculation.
At that time, the king ascended the tower and spoke these words:
"It is because of evil desires that people commit evil deeds. Such desires are like a corpse walking through a latrine filled with filth; how can one commit evil for their sake!"

Fools covet kingdoms and give rise to a competitive and contentious mind, just as a flock of birds scramble and quarrel over a piece of meat. These sentient beings are constantly beset by enmity and hatred—namely old age, sickness, and death—and yet how can they fail to observe these enemies within themselves, instead giving rise to contention toward others?
While King Sarvadarśin was contemplating this matter, the hostile and vengeful king entered the palace.
At that moment, the king escaped through a water drain and fled into the deep mountains; reaching a dense forest, he managed to evade his enemies.
The ground is pure, with various kinds of trees and immeasurable flowers and fruits beyond calculation;
the water is clear and soft, endowed with the eight virtues, and there are countless birds—ducks and geese—and beasts.
Having seen this, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he spoke again: “I have now truly escaped the faults and afflictions of the household life.

Countless sentient beings are constantly oppressed by the terrors of old age, sickness, and death; yet now I have attained this place of pure peace and happiness, beyond description. This forest is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas who cultivate compassion, and it is also the firm and impregnable fortress for those who destroy the four Māras. Having now obtained a pure bath and freed myself from all defilements, I am now a companion to these deer; my body and mind are secure, and I experience the highest bliss.”
At that time, once the hostile king had seized his kingdom, he immediately issued a proclamation to search for the former king:

"If anyone can capture King Sarvamdada—whether by killing him or binding him and bringing him here—I shall grant them a heavy reward, providing whatever they may require. Since he formerly used to praise himself as one who could practice the True Dharma while reviling us for our tyrannical and evil conduct, I now wish to see him so that I may demonstrate to him the fruits obtained from practicing goodness."
At that time, there was a brahmin from another region who was impoverished and destitute, surviving solely by begging; moreover, he had encountered legal trouble and had no one to rely upon.
Having heard the king’s name—that he delighted in practicing charity—they came from their own country, desiring to approach him to beg for whatever they required.
On the way, exhausted by hunger and thirst, they stopped in a forest grove and immediately slandered him, saying:

"This place is a tranquil abode for sages; it is also where divine seers and those free from desire dwell. Those seeking liberation here abstain from food and drink; they do not keep slaves or servants, nor do they ride in carriages or on horses. Having few desires and being content, they eat only millet, tubers, and medicinal herbs."

This is the dwelling place of those who possess the mind of great compassion, and it is also a place where all birds and beasts are free from fear; the Sovereign King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven manifested this place in order to cause sentient beings to perceive the faults and afflictions of the household life.
At that time, having heard these words, King Sarvamdada felt great joy in his heart; he went at once to see him, exchanged greetings with him, and invited him to sit.
Then the brahmin immediately sat down before him; once seated, King Sarvamdada offered him all the various sweet fruits he possessed.
Once he had finished eating his fill, the king immediately asked: "Great Brahmin!
This place is fearsome and devoid of people; it is a solitary dwelling for those who practice the path in quiet seclusion. For what reason have you come here?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "You should not ask me about this matter.
You are a person of merit and purity who has distanced yourself from the confinement and fetters of the household; for what reason do you ask me such a thing?"
You should not hear such turbid and evil sounds: "If another offends me, I shall offend him;
if another robs me, I shall rob him. Because of living as a householder, one suffers such things as the loss of wealth and the decline of one's kin.
"Virtuous One!
You have now severed all fetters and dwell in the mountain forests, as free and unimpeded as a great nāga-elephant.
The Bodhisattva Sarvamdada then spoke these words:
"The words you have now spoken are pure and gentle; why do you not dwell together with us here?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "If you wish to hear it, I shall explain it to you in full detail."

My place of birth was far removed from here; due to my meager merit, I encountered a tyrannical king who was like a lion amidst a herd of deer, never possessing even a single thought of kindness or compassion.
My king is likewise cruel and tyrannical; he has no compassion for his subjects, and whether one is guilty or innocent, he acts solely according to his greed for wealth.

Since my birth, I have been cautious and reverent, never having committed even a hair’s breadth of offense against the royal laws; yet he has arbitrarily seized my home and cast me into prison, demanding fifty pieces of gold from me:
"If you can provide this, I shall pardon your domestic transgressions."
"If you refuse to pay, I will never let you go; you shall certainly be bound, imprisoned, and flogged.
He set a date for the payment of the gold coins, but the family was so impoverished and destitute that they had no means to provide for it.

I have heard that in this land there was a King Universal Giver who delighted in practicing charity to protect and sustain the poor; his acts of giving were never interrupted, like the continuous succession of flowers and fruits on a tree during spring and summer, or like the cool, clear water in a wilderness where a thirsty person who encounters it may drink to their heart's content;

or like a great assembly where no one can stop anyone from participating. To speak briefly now, even if a person had a thousand heads, each head a thousand mouths, each mouth a thousand tongues, and each tongue capable of explaining a thousand meanings, they could not exhaustively praise all the virtues of this king.
That king has achieved such fame and virtue.

Now that I live as a householder, I have encountered the king’s tyranny; I am unjustly beset by guilt and have no one else to rely upon. Therefore, I wish to go before him to petition for what I require.
Nevertheless, this thought has constantly been in my mind:
"When shall I go to his place and beg as I wish?
If that Great King would surely look upon me with compassion and grant me even a small amount, my family could preserve its life; if I do not obtain it, I too shall soon perish."
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva’s heart was overwhelmed and he fell to the ground, like a great tree toppled by a violent wind.
Then, the brahmin immediately sprinkled cold water upon the king’s body, and he regained consciousness.
Then the brahmin asked again:
"Great Seer!
Upon hearing that my family is undergoing such suffering and distress, has your mind not become bewildered and distressed?"

"In this state of purity, you who are so dear to me have been able to give rise to a heart of compassion; even when I encountered such a situation, I felt no sorrow or suffering—by what cause do you now give rise to such distress?"
The king replied:
"You originally intended to visit that king; however, due to your meager fortune, you encountered him when he was away. If you go now, you will certainly not see him, which is why I am grieved."
At that time, the brahmin asked,
"Where has he gone? King Dāna replied:
"There was a king whose enemy came to seize his kingdom; now, having fled for his life, he dwells in the empty mountain forests, with only birds and beasts as his companions."
When the brahmin heard these words, he immediately fainted again.
King Sarvamdada once more sprinkled him with cold water to bring him back to consciousness, and then comforted him, saying:
"You may sit now; do not grieve or suffer."
The brahmin said,
"Today my life will certainly not be preserved. Why is this?"
"What I originally sought and prayed for has now all been destroyed; how can I possibly rise?
I shall surely give up my life.
At that moment, King Sarvamdada immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion and thought thus:

"The aspirations of this pitiable practitioner have not been fulfilled; he is like a hungry ghost who sees clear water from afar but, upon reaching it, finds it cannot be obtained, his heart becoming so distressed that he collapses to the ground. This Brahmin is just the same."
Again he called out to him, saying:
"Ho, Brahmin! You may rise and sit; you may rise and sit."
"The King who gave all things is none other than my own self.
You originally wished to see him, and now you have encountered him; why then do you grieve?
The brāhmaṇa asked the king:
"Now you have comforted me with kind words; do you have any wealth?
The king replied, "I have no wealth, but I possess a skillful means by which you may obtain great treasures."
The brahmin asked,
"What means [should be employed]?
The king replied once more:
"I have previously heard that an enemy residing in my kingdom has proclaimed these words before the great assembly:
'If anyone can capture King Sarvamdada, or take his life and bring him bound here, I shall grant them a heavy reward according to their every desire.'"
"Since time immemorial, I have never taught anyone to practice unwholesome dharmas; therefore, do not cut off my head, but merely bind me with ropes and deliver me to that king."
Why is this? Apart from the body, there is no other wealth.
However, as I now have mastery over this body, it would be fortunate if it could be exchanged for wealth to provide mutual relief.
Excellent, excellent! O Brahmin!
I have now gained great benefit, having exchanged this non-durable body for a durable one.

"Daoist, observe this: even if my body were to meet its end here, my corpse would be cast into the wilderness no different from grass or wood; though birds and beasts might come to devour it, what benefit would there be in that?"
"Now that I have traded this body of dust and ash for genuine gold and precious treasures, how could I possibly feel any attachment or regret?
When the Brahmin heard these words, he wept with grief and said,
"How can such a principle exist?"

Why is this? You are now the unsurpassed tamer, the father and mother of sentient beings, the excellent protector and great refuge; you are able to extinguish all the fears of immeasurable sentient beings. Your deeds are vast and you do not expect any recompense; you always give rise to compassion for all sentient beings and are able to act as a great lamp in this dark age.
"How could I destroy the True Dharma and bind your body to send you to the enemy king?
Even if I were to bring the king to that enemy and obtain gold and jewels in return, with what state of mind would I stretch out my hand to accept them?"
If one were to accept it, one's hands would fall to the ground;
it is like a man who, for the sake of nourishing his own body, eats the flesh of his parents—though he may thereby preserve his life, how is he any different from an enemy?
"I am likewise; even if I were to bind the king's body and deliver him to that enemy, though I might gain great wealth to ransom my home and family, I would not value it.
Then the king replied, "What need is there to deliberate further on such words?"
"If you truly feel compassion for me, I shall bind myself and follow behind you to that enemy; you will incur no fault, and I shall gain merit."
The brahmin said,
"I shall respectfully follow Your Majesty’s command and act according to your will.
Having spoken these words, the king immediately bound himself and, accompanied by the brahmin, proceeded to the city.
When the king’s former ministers and the people saw him, they were all struck with wonder and said:
"Alas, Brahmin! You are a rākṣasa, not a brahmin; you are a rākṣasa, not a brahmin!"

"You were originally a truly violent and malevolent ghost-spirit, deceitfully manifesting the appearance of a Brahmin; lacking any heart of compassion, you are truly the Death-Mara who constantly seeks to kill people."

You have now caused this king’s body to perish and vanish, like an eclipse of the moon; as if seven suns were to shine simultaneously and the great ocean were to dry up, the unsurpassed lamp of the Dharma is extinguished today. O outcaste, how is it that your hand does not fall to the ground?
Why does your body not sink into the earth?
Once a lion king has died, who is unable to harm him?
King Sarvamdada has long since abandoned his kingdom, city, wife, children, granaries, treasures, and all contention; he has retired to the deep mountains to cultivate the practice of quiescence.
"What offense have you committed against us that you have brought this upon us?
The people of the entire city raised their voices in unison, praying:
"O Great Sages and Holy Ones! O Four World-Protecting Kings!"
"I pray that you will add your majestic power to protect this king and ensure his life remains whole.
When the brahmin heard these words, fear arose in his heart; he took Sarvamdada and hastened to the king's presence, speaking thus:
"Great King, you should know that I have now obtained King Sarvamdada."
When the hostile king saw this, a thought immediately arose in his mind:
"This king is in the prime of youth; his body is handsome, his features are upright, and his strength is difficult to restrain.
This brahmin, however, is advanced in years; his appearance is withered and haggard, his countenance is ugly, and he possesses little strength. How could he possibly bring this king here?"
I then privately gave rise to this thought:
"Could this not be Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, Nārāyaṇa, or one of the Four Heavenly Kings?"
The hostile king then asked,
"Who bound you?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I bound myself!
the resentful king cursed, saying:
"Begone, you fool!"
He asked again:
"Are you not binding him by the power of incantations?
Your body is weak and frail, while his body is majestic like that of Śakra; how could you possibly bind him?"
Suppose there were someone who said of themselves:
"I can blow Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, until it is reduced to fine powder.
Would this be credible?
At that time, King Vairambha immediately addressed his ministers:
"You should know: is this present difficulty a dream, or is it a magical illusion?"
"Is it not that my mind has become faint and my will lost, such that I have seen this through a delusion?
How could this old monkey bind the body of Śakra?
Your ministers should know: how could the fibers within a lotus root support Mount Sumeru?"
"Can one cross the great ocean by means of a rabbit's body?
Can one exhaust the depths of the sea with the tip of a mosquito's proboscis?
When the brāhmaṇa heard these words, he immediately addressed King Vairasena with a verse:
"Great King, you should now know: I truly could not have been bound;
it was because of Your Majesty’s compassion that You came here for my sake.
It would be as difficult as trying to catch the wind in a net—this matter is exceedingly hard to accomplish."
"Even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, could not do this for you.
At that time, King Vairasena spoke these words to King Sarvadada:

"Out of compassion for me, you have entered the deep mountains, valleys, forests, and desolate places, where you enjoy only the company of birds and beasts; with few desires and contentment, you drink water and eat fruit, using grass as a mat, and no longer contend with me."
"However, my resentment has not yet been extinguished; I now possess the power to execute you. For what reason have you come here?
At that time, King Sarvadada smiled with delight, free from all fear, his body and mind as relaxed and majestic as a lion king, and he spoke these words:
"Do you not know?!"
I am indeed named King Sarvamdada; it is because I wish to fulfill my original vow that I have now come here for three reasons:
first, to seek wealth on behalf of a brahmin.
Second, because you previously offered a reward, saying that whoever brings my body here shall be heavily rewarded;
third, because I have long held a vow to practice universal giving, I have therefore come wishing to sacrifice my own life.
"You should now consider this: if this body of mine were to end its life and enter the earth, what benefit would it bring?
The reason I originally fled into the mountain forests was not out of fear, but solely to love and protect all sentient beings."

"You now possess the power, yet your heart of enmity has not been extinguished. If I were to come here now and slaughter you at my will, I would thereby eliminate the resentment and find peace of mind; therefore, you should do so yourself early."
Then he spoke these verses:
"To harbor resentment toward an enemy Is to scorch one's own mind;
Just like a fire beneath the ashes, It is still capable of burning all things."
Because the mind clings to hatred, at the end of life one falls into hell;
it is like a poisoned arrow, which destroys both body and life as soon as it strikes.
If one harbors anger toward those who are hateful, the mind finds no tranquility.
Just as one with a painful eye cannot see true colors,
so this body is composed of flesh and blood, marrow, bone, fat, grease, and brain,
along with excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva, all wrapped over by a thin skin.
This body is like a walking latrine; it has no master and no self.
What grievance do you have against the King that you constantly give rise to anger?
The thieves of birth, old age, sickness, and death are constantly coming to invade the King’s person.
Why, in this situation, do you instead give rise to thoughts of kinship and friendship?
My body is composed of the four great elements, and the King’s body is likewise so.
If you now perceive anger, it is in fact anger directed at yourself.

"Therefore, Great King, you should not give rise to anger; if you must be angry, since you now possess the power of authority, it would be fortunate if you could execute me at your pleasure as soon as possible.
As for those previously offered as rewards, they may be granted to this man;
as for me, I shall certainly sacrifice my life without regret."
“By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings be able to practice universal giving and attain the name of ‘The One Who Gives All.
At that time, having heard these words, King Vairambha rose from his royal throne, joined his palms in respectful salutation to King Sarvamdada, and spoke thus:
“I pray only this, Great King!
I return to my original seat. You are the Dharma King, the sovereign of true transformation; I am a rākṣasa of violent and evil nature.
You are the Lamp of the World, the parent of the world; I am a base and wicked great thief in this world, who exclusively practices evil dharmas to plunder the wealth of others.
You are the Righteous Dharma Mirror of Dharmakīrti; I am one of "unrighteous fame" who constantly deceives others, like a blind man who does not recognize his own faults.

"Since our transgressions are so deep and heavy, this body of ours ought to have long since sunk into this earth. That we have been able to linger until this day is truly due to the support provided by your honor; we now relinquish this ground and offer our very bodies to you."

King Sarvamdada then extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for King Vairambha, establishing him firmly within the True Dharma; he then bestowed vast wealth and treasures upon the brahmin and sent him back to his own land.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in this manner, they relinquish even such a highly cherished body, let alone external possessions and wealth.
For the sake of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not fail to bestow as a gift anything among all that he holds dear.
As I have heard in the past:
In the past, there was a king who had a son named Sarvadhara.

Though he was young in years, his physical form was upright and handsome, like the full moon shining brightly among the stars; sentient beings gazed upon him without ever feeling satiated. His majestic demeanor was calm and stable, like Mount Sumeru;
his wisdom was profoundly deep, like the great ocean.
Accomplished in patience, he is like the great earth;
his mind is unchanging, like Jāmbūnada gold, and is always beloved by all humans and devas.
Like water of eight virtues, pure and clear, his mind is impartial toward all in the world;
like the sun and moon, which shine equally upon all things, he fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings;
and like a wish-fulfilling jewel, he feels joy in his heart whenever he beholds those who come to him for alms.
It was like a compassionate mother seeing her beloved child.
At that time, the prince spoke these verses:
"I have now attained sovereignty, And possess immeasurable wealth."
He shares everything with all sentient beings, like the sun that shines equally upon all.
When he sees those who come to beg, he never says there is nothing;
even to those who seek nothing, he likewise gives.
The prince-bodhisattva’s faculties were tranquil, like those of Brahmā;
he was fully endowed with wealth and treasures, like Vaiśravaṇa.
For the sake of all sentient beings, the king served as their attendant and messenger, just as a disciple serves his teacher or preceptor.
His mind constantly cherishes and remembers all sentient beings, just as parents cherish the children they have borne;
he teaches and transforms sentient beings through the rules of Dharma and propriety, like a great master teacher.

The Prince-Bodhisattva has fully accomplished such merits as these; his mind always delights in bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings, thinking, "I shall give such an object to this person, and such an object to so-and-so";
and when this person is terrified, he shall comfort them, practicing the True Dharma without ever abandoning it.

As for the things bestowed, they include gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musaragalva, agate, coral, jade, and various utensils; as well as clothing, beds, bedding, vehicles, houses, fields, grain, slaves, servants, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—whatever may be required, he is able to provide it in full sufficiency.
Just as the rain from heaven causes the hundred grains to flourish, he constantly bestows wealth and goods with his five fingers,
like five dragons pouring down a great rain.
This prince-bodhisattva always practices giving, never ceasing day by day.

Suppose that for a single day no one comes to beg; his complexion becomes withered and haggard, and his heart is filled with sorrow and distress, like the crescent moon shrouded by mist and fog, devoid of radiance.
At that time, all the ministers conceived feelings of resentment toward this prince, saying: "Alas!
Our king is foolish and lacks wisdom; possessing wealth yet not enjoying it himself, where will he find peace in the next life?
Seeing [the prince's] conduct, he neither employs him nor rebukes his son, instead distributing the treasury to those who have rendered no service."
When the treasuries are exhausted, the people shall disperse; once the people have dispersed, resentment will arise—who will protect them?
If there is no protection, life cannot be preserved; if life is not preserved, who will remain in the land?
At that time, the great ministers and the people each reflected upon these matters.

At that time, the father-king possessed a white elephant that could walk upon lotus flowers; its strength was such that it could subdue the enemies and adversaries of rival nations, and because he possessed this elephant, other kingdoms were unable to invade or oppress him.
At that time, there was a king who was an enemy from a border region and constantly thought to himself:
"By what means and expedient might I obtain that white elephant?
He immediately dispatched several men, disguised as ascetic brahmins, to go to the prince and request the white elephant.

At that time, because the prince had conceived feelings of anger toward the various ministers, he mounted a white elephant and left the city to go sightseeing, intending to head toward a certain grove; it was along that path that he saw a brahmin.
Upon seeing the prince, his heart was filled with great joy, and he offered this prayer:
"May the prince succeed to the unsurpassed throne of the Great King; may his lifespan be immeasurable;
may neighboring states submit to his virtue, and may all under heaven enjoy peace."
"O Prince!

We are all brahmins dwelling in distant lands. Because we have long heard of your fondness for giving, we have come from afar; yet on the road, we have suffered many hardships from hunger and thirst."
"Prince! You should know that we uphold the pure precepts and have extensively studied and recited the scriptures, leaving nothing unmastered.

Your virtues, Prince, spread throughout the ten directions; hearing of your reputation and praising you, there are none who do not rejoice. You are able to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings, and no one who comes to beg returns empty-handed. We pray that you will grant us the elephant upon which you ride."
At that time, the prince thought to himself:
"If I do not give it now, I shall violate my original vow;
yet if I were to give it, it is not mine to own, for it is something my father the King holds dear and precious."
He then spoke to them, saying:
"Gentlemen, if you require gold, silver, lapis lazuli, various types of carriages, or the like of slaves and servants, I am able to provide all of these;

however, as for this white elephant, it is not mine to command and is not under my control. Furthermore, it is the very elephant upon which my royal father rides. How could I possibly bestow it upon you as a gift?"
"Calculate how much this white elephant is worth; I shall provide the price so as not to leave you in want.
Why must you insist on having this white elephant?"

"O Brahmin! Out of compassion for sentient beings, you have left the household life and received the precepts, having already distanced yourself from all material things; what use have you for this elephant?
If you were to possess it, there might well be further affliction."
The brahmins spoke again, saying:

"We do not require money or precious treasures; we only need this elephant to ride into the mountains. Having sought out excellent flowers to make offerings to the various devas, we shall cause sentient beings to be reborn in the heavens or enter nirvāṇa."
"The Prince’s original vow was to benefit others, and I likewise desire to benefit others.
At that time, having heard these words, the Prince immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion; he then descended from the white elephant and thought to himself:

"Although this elephant belongs to my father the King, if I now give it as a gift, the ministers and the people will surely look upon me with disdain. In desiring to benefit others, how can I allow myself to calculate such things!"
"However, my giving does not seek fame or rebirth among gods or humans; by these causes and conditions, I shall cause all sentient beings to sever their afflictions.
Having made this vow, he then gave the white elephant to the brahmin and, mounting a single horse himself, returned toward the city.
Once the brahmins had obtained the elephant, they mounted it together and returned home.
In an instant, they arrived back in their own country.
At that time, the ministers gathered together and went quickly to the king’s presence, saying:
"Great King!

Today, the noble white elephant you so highly prize has been taken by the prince and given as a gift to the brahmins. Having received it, the brahmins have mounted it and departed for the enemy kingdom.
Because you did not rebuke him when you previously witnessed his giving of gold, silver, and precious jewels, he has now caused you to give away even this white elephant to your enemies."
"Great King!

The wicked sons of this world are full of many faults and afflictions; they drink wine, gamble, lust after women, and squander wealth. We venture to report this, yet we do not seek to reproach you. If the prince, from this day forward, no longer bestows wealth as gifts upon others, then he may be permitted to remain;
if he does not desist, he must be banished to dwell in the remote deep mountains."
At that time, the father-king immediately summoned his son and thought to himself:
"How strange!
Why have all these ministers today suddenly prevented my son from practicing charity as he pleases?"
"I am now filled with shame, just like a woman who fears her mother-in-law.
He then spoke these words to his son:
"From this day forward, you must no longer be greedily attached; you should abandon all meritorious attachments."
"One who practices the True Dharma should wear garments of grass, eat wild fruits, and dwell in remote deep mountains;
you should not now gouge out your right eye to treat your left. How is it that today, all at once, you have disturbed my mind and those of the great ministers?"
As for the way of humanity, one first establishes one's own kin and only then should one extend it to others; why do you now propose to give my white elephant as a gift to an enemy?

In the *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, Volume One, on the right side of the third folio, line fourteen, beneath the phrase "the majestic power of the deer herd," the Dan edition contains the following: "As I have heard, in the past, due to the causal conditions of anger, the Bodhisattva fell among the dragons; even when the five grains were about to ripen, he encountered evil hail from the heavens, and so forth."
This comprises twenty-six lines and four hundred and forty-two characters;
those portions absent from the Guo and Song editions have now been verified against the original text and are found in the lower fascicle of this very sutra.
The passage from the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on the Dragon" (*Nāga-varga*), has been erroneously misplaced here in the *Danzang* (the Tibetan Tripitaka);
therefore, it is not accepted here. Composed by Saṃghasena, the *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, middle fascicle.
Translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian (style name Gongming) of Wu.
The Remainder of Chapter Three: The Prince Sarvasattva. At that time, the prince joined his palms, knelt with bended knees, and paid respectful homage to his father, the King, saying:

"The alms I have bestowed were not for the sake of greed, hatred, or delusion; nor was it for the sake of fame and reputation, nor to seek birth among the wealthy and noble within the realms of gods or humans. It was not an act committed with a mind of madness or derangement, but was performed as an offering for the sake of seeking the True Dharma."
"Great King!
You should know that although I now protect my parents, brothers, wife, and children, at the time of death, even though I have kinsmen, who can follow me?"
I see only that the True Dharma pursues me and will not abandon me.

If I were one who lacked the intent to practice the wholesome Dharma, I might still hope for Your Majesty’s stern words of admonition; how could you, all of a sudden, believe and act upon these perverse words, thereby severing my practice of goodness?

The King first commanded his minister to relinquish the mind of renunciation. "But this mind of renunciation," the minister replied, "is my fundamental nature and original source; how can it be relinquished?
It is like the nature of earth, whose solidity cannot be relinquished;
even so, the nature of fire, whose heat cannot be relinquished."
Like a fish cast onto dry land, how could its life possibly endure?

Though this man possesses the six sense-faculties like a king’s servant and his physical body is as complete as anyone else’s, differing not from the heavens, how can such a person serve as an attendant to the king?
From where did all the royal carriages, court ladies, gold, silver, and precious jewels originate?
One should know that these are all the results of past acts of giving, now received as retribution.
"Great King!
You should know that all hungry ghosts, being oppressed by the fire of hunger, have bodies and minds scorched with distress; all such states are caused by the conditions of greed and stinginess.
As for those among the devas who possess palaces of the seven treasures and enjoy long lifespans, you should know that these are all caused by the conditions of generosity."
"Great King!

What I have now given as a gift cannot be burned by fire, nor can it be swept away by water; neither the thieves and robbers of the royal household, nor enemies or creditors, can seize or plunder these gifted objects."
Among all realms of existence, he acts as a kinsman and friend; this celestial vehicle is that which carries the gifts bestowed;
within the cycle of birth and death, it follows the body of the servant, just as a calf follows its mother.
"As the King has commanded, you are to cease this mind of giving; if you cannot relinquish it, you shall be exiled to the deep mountains.
Even if you reach the deep mountains, as long as your mind of giving does not cease, impoverished people will likewise come to you."
"Your servant’s original vow was indeed to delight in the mountain forests; the reason I did not petition you before was that I feared my father would not grant permission.
Now that Your Majesty has granted leave, I have truly attained my original wish. I shall now take my leave and set out upon the road immediately."
Why is this? These mountain forests are secluded places favored by sages and saints, where one can abandon greed, hatred, and delusion; if I go there, he will surely be able to benefit himself.
At that time, the prince prostrated at the king’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, took his leave, and departed;
he then went to his mother’s quarters, knelt and prostrated as was customary, circumambulated her three times to the right, and after paying homage at her feet, departed;
finally, he went to his wife’s quarters and spoke these words:
"May you dwell here in peace, supporting your parents and protecting your son; this is precisely how you shall practice the True Dharma.
Now I wish to depart and travel far into the mountain forests."
Why is this? It has been my constant wish from the beginning to enter the deep mountains to cultivate my resolve.
Now that the King, my father, grants me leave, I shall go there with all speed to fulfill my heart's desire.
"You shall be a companion among the birds and beasts, subsisting on fruits and water to sustain yourself;
you are a princess, with a body so delicate, upright, and refined—how could you endure such bitter hardships? Therefore, you should remain here and need not follow me."

Upon hearing this, his wife was overcome with distress and anguish; her body trembled like the leaves of a plantain tree. She wailed and wept, beating her breast and tearing out her hair, crying out in a loud voice:
"Alas! What is to be done!"
"What crime have you committed that the King, your father, has banished you to these deep mountains?

Your Majesty is broad-minded and compassionate, governing according to the True Dharma and loving the people as if they were your own children; why then have you suddenly driven us away in such a manner?"
"You cherish your physical form; your complexion is as soft and supple as the *campaka* flower. How can you suddenly lie upon thorns, stones, and earth?
Now you enjoy yourself within the palace amidst the five sensory pleasures; were you to enter the mountains, you would hear only the harsh cries of tigers, wolves, lions, and other venomous beasts."
How strange!
Where is the King’s heart of compassion today?
How has a father become so estranged and cold, turning into an enemy over such a trivial cause all at once?
At that time, the prince replied to his wife,
saying: "Excellent,
O Princess!
"You possess profound wisdom, diligence, and valor; you are my virtuous companion. Even if I were not right, I should have rebuked you; why then do you utter such coarse words?"

"When kings wage war against one another for the sake of their kingdoms, it is all due to the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; this is my auspicious karmic condition, which has caused my father the king to permit me to enter the mountains to practice the True Dharma. You should not now give rise to displeasure."

It is a constant law of the world that when a king grows old and infirm, he establishes his crown prince to oversee the affairs of state. Since state affairs are complex and fraught with many faults, once those faults have fallen upon one's own person, there is no place of escape.

Your Majesty is not yet in decline, yet you are already able to relinquish [the throne] and grant me permission to enter the mountains to cultivate my resolve; thus, the faults of the world shall never again reach me. Why, then, do you not rejoice?
"You may stay here as you please; I now wish to depart.
She replied, "When my parents gave me to you, the sun, the moon, the great earth, and the Four Heavenly Kings were all witnesses."
On the day of our first marriage, you yourself spoke these words, vowing never to forsake me; how can you now wish to go alone?
You should know that the sun and moon, as well as the fierce fire, are inseparable from their own light and substance; why then do you now wish to abandon me?

At that time, the prince gave away all his family wealth in alms to the poor and destitute; he then took his two sons upon his shoulders, led his wife by the hand, and departed for the Snowy Mountains.
When the prince arrived, he sustained his life by eating fruit and drinking water, practicing the mind of loving-kindness and compassion day and night. He further thought to himself:

"Although I formerly lived at home and experienced the five desires, they were not like the joy I find today dwelling in these mountains. Such happiness as this surpasses even the sensual pleasures enjoyed by Śakra Devānām Indra."
"These sentient beings do not know the subtle flavor of the True Dharma, just as a crow does not know the flavor of the lotus.
At that time, the prince constantly contemplated this meaning for the sake of sentient beings, while his wife regularly entered the mountains to gather fruits and melons to provide for them.
At that time, there was an old Brahmin of hideous appearance whom people loathed to look upon, who arrived from a distant land.
Upon seeing him, the prince immediately bade him sit, provided him with water and fruit, and then inquired:
"For what reason have you come here?"
"Is this not because you have grown weary of the faults of the household life?

In your youth, you should have remained at home and indulged to the full in the five desires; now that you are aged and infirm and the time of death is approaching, it is truly a joyous matter to renounce everything and come to practice the Way."
"This place is secluded and free from the faults of household life; if you take pleasure in this, I shall constantly provide you with sweet fruits and cool water so that you never lack for anything."
The brahmin said:
"One who is free from thoughts of desire should dwell here; as for me, I have not yet been able to extinguish thoughts of desire, and therefore I cannot dwell here."
"Great Seer! Behold this:

although my body is old—with white hair, fallen teeth, trembling steps, and blurred vision; with a parched tongue and dry mouth that cannot speak; with a head so heavy it is difficult to bear, like Mount Tai; and with ears that no longer hear clearly as my physical faculties have decayed—I still possess desires just as when I was in my prime."
"O Great Sage!

You should know that I am advanced in years, my physical strength is diminished, and my household is impoverished and destitute, burdened by the labor of servants. If you wish to fulfill my original aspiration, I would be grateful if you would kindly grant me two slave-servants."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately thought:
"How strange!
If it is said today that [the fruit] does not exist, then this contradicts my original vow."
"If you say there is [wealth], why are you now truly empty and poor?
The brāhmaṇa said, "Why do you hesitate now? What are you contemplating?"
"You might wonder whether I am a Brahmin who upholds the prohibitive precepts and is a man of extensive learning;
if you have such a doubt, I am indeed so.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"When I was formerly at home, I had many servants and attendants, and my stores of gold, silver, and precious jewels were overflowing.

At that time, whenever I saw a beggar, I never said I had nothing; yet now, staying here, I have brought none of it with me. Where could I possibly find enough to match what is required? This is why I hesitate and contemplate this matter."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I am now old and decrepit, my strength exhausted; I have come from afar to beg for what I require. From the time you were born, whenever you have seen a beggar, you have never once spoken the words:
'I have nothing.'"
"For what reason do you speak such words today?
Great Seer!
If you would compassionately grant us these two slaves, I shall return to my kingdom."
"If you cannot do so, I shall surely die here.
At that time, the prince immediately thought to himself:
"What skillful means should I now employ to send this man away?"
At that time, the two sons were playing nearby in the mountains not far away, and they again thought to themselves:
"We shall now act as the cause and condition for all sentient beings so that their efforts are not in vain."
He immediately summoned his sons; once they had arrived, the Bodhisattva embraced them and thought again: "My two sons have grown up within the deep seclusion of the palace;
their bodies are delicate and tender, having never experienced the hardships of cold. How can I suddenly cause them to part from their parents to become servants to another?"
He further thought:
"For what reason do I now conceive such thoughts? If I do not practice difficult and arduous austerities, by what means could I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
For these reasons, I shall practice this; by virtue of this practice, may I swiftly attain the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

I now renounce these two beloved sons of mine, not seeking the karmic rewards of rebirth among gods or humans, nor the status of a Cakravartin king, Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings; I vow that through this merit, all sentient beings may together achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took his two children in his hands and handed them over to the brahmin, saying:

"O brahmin! These two children of mine are like my own life. They are young and without wisdom; they do not yet understand human speech. Though they appear to be human, they possess no discernment. I now give them to you to serve as your servants. I fear my wife may arrive, so you should take them away quickly."
At that time, the two sons turned back and grasped their father’s robes, saying to him:
"Father, for what reason do you now give us, your sons and brothers, to this wicked brahmin?"
"From this day forward, we shall be forever separated from our parents; being so young in years and lacking any worldly knowledge, how can we survive without protection or guardianship?
For what reason must we endure such suffering?"

"Now that we have fallen into the hands of others, our lives will surely not be preserved; just as one who violates the king's law receives punishment, we are but ignorant and small beings who have committed no offense—by what cause do we encounter such suffering today?"
If even those who have actually committed an offense still hope for forgiveness and release, how much more so for one who has committed no wrong and yet is falsely accused?

Even if my father’s heart of affection for me were severed, it would still be improper according to human law to act thus; for such things occur among the old and the young, and among the foolish and the wise alike. Why does my father now treat me with such particular bitterness and cruelty?
If one were to abandon others for the sake of the Dharma, would such a loss of compassion truly be the Dharma?

Although I am young, I have also heard it said that according to the Brahmanical law, if one protects one's wife and children through such causes and conditions, one may be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva’s body and mind trembled, and he immediately reproached himself:
“For what reason has this come to pass?
Does your mind not know better!”
Since time immemorial, among all sentient beings wandering through birth and death, who has not been an enemy?
Who has not been a child?
Are you now so shrouded in darkness and blind that you have no vision?
Why do you not focus your mindfulness to contemplate and discern?
Now that you have merely been taken away from your two children, you are already shaken like this!
When the time of death arrives, what will you do then?
At that time, having rebuked his mind, the Bodhisattva immediately attained a state of stable composure and said to the brahmin,
"Take them away quickly. Then,
the two sons addressed their father, saying:
"Listen! Stay a moment;
it will not be too late for me to depart after my mother has arrived, and I have paid my respects and taken my leave.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"You two simply go on ahead; we, along with your mother, shall follow behind you.
At that time, the brahmin led his two sons and set out with great haste.
At that time, the two sons followed along the road, looking back and gazing upon their father’s face, wailing and weeping piteously.
The Bodhisattva then further admonished his own mind: "You should no longer tremble or be shaken;

you must contemplate how this embodied existence is ablaze with old age and death. Before the sons had gone far, he again established a vow: "My abandoning my children now is indeed a difficult practice. By virtue of these causes and conditions, may I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and sever all the fetters of sentient beings."
At that time, not long after the brahmin had set out on his way, he thought to himself:

"How extraordinary is this prince! He is a rarity in the world; he acts exactly as he speaks, having bestowed his two children upon me, and the wholesome dharmas he has cultivated are fully perfected."
"Now where shall we sell these two children?
We have no choice but to return to our ancestral kingdom.
At that time, the brahmin immediately took the two children and went to the royal palace. When the ancestral king saw his two grandsons, grief and joy welled up within him, and he asked the brahmin:
"From where did you obtain these two children?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "Listen!
"In those Snowy Mountains, there was a son of a great king named Sarvadhara; he has given these two sons to me to be my slaves.
Upon hearing these words, the king wrung his hands and said, "How strange!
How extraordinary!"
"My son loves the Dharma so excessively that he has not even spared his beloved child;
return him to me now, and I shall pay you the price.
The Brahmin said:
“I respectfully obey Your Majesty’s command. She immediately accepted the precious jewels and returned to her home.

At that time, while the Bodhisattva’s wife was in a forest clearing, her left eye twitched; her heart was startled and she felt uneasy. The various flowers she had gathered withered and dried up instantly, and two fruits from her basket sprang out and fell to the ground. Her two breasts throbbed and milk flowed out of their own accord. A bird appeared before her and cried out repeatedly. She then thought to herself:
"This present omen must surely be inauspicious; could it be that my husband's life-force has been severed?
Or perhaps a tiger, a wolf, a lion, or some other fierce beast has devoured my son?"
"Or has he gone out for recreation and fallen from a mountain to his death?
Having thought this, she returned to her dwelling and soon saw the Bodhisattva near a rocky shore, sitting with his body leaning forward upon a grass mat.
She then thought: "My husband is here; surely there is no cause for concern."
He then stepped forward and said,
"Are your two sons now at peace?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The two children are safe.
The wife spoke again, saying,
"I have indeed heard with my own ears that they are safe, yet because I have not seen them, I still harbor grief and sorrow."
The Bodhisattva replied, "Just sit down for a moment; you shall see it for yourself.
His wife then withdrew to sit, and he spoke to her again:
"Do you not know my original vow? Whatever I possess must be given to others.
After you had gone out this morning, a brahmin came to beg from me, and I immediately gave my two children as alms."
Upon hearing these words, his wife’s mind was overwhelmed; she threw herself down, fell to the ground, and fainted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva sprinkled water upon her; after being sprinkled with water, she regained consciousness. Her body trembled as she sat and spoke this verse: "How strange!
For the sake of the True Dharma, I have practiced such ascetic austerities."
When giving away your son, how was your mind not disturbed?
Your heart is not made of steel, nor have you forever severed your affection;
how could you possibly take your son and give him away to another?
My son, though yet young, is peerless in his upright beauty;
his countenance is like a lotus, and his eyes are like blue utpala flowers.
He feeds himself on wild fruits and does not trouble others with his needs.
How can one be so devoid of human feeling as to give [this] away to another all at once?
This path is full of stones and sand, thorns, and wicked brambles;
where will that person, lacking both compassion and wisdom, lead you?
Do you not see now!
Even those deer and other such creatures still come seeking and searching; how much more so for you, who are their father?
Do you not see all the trees within this mountain?
Because they have lost their children, they all weep aloud;
even all the trees, which possess no consciousness,
can still do this— how much more so those who possess minds?
At that time, there was a plantain tree on the ground whose entire body trembled;
his wife immediately said to him, "Even your husband has given away his own offspring to others—is he not compassionate?"
"Why is it that you are thus trembling with your whole body?
