At that time, his wife, grieving and wailing for her son, ran hither and thither, finding no peace in her place.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Excellent, excellent!
Having already entered the mountains to practice the wholesome Dharma, why do you allow your mind to undergo such suffering?"
To have lived in seclusion and cultivated the sublime principles of goodness in vain—how strange it is, O Princess!

Though you possess profound wisdom and courageous diligence, you are unable to understand the perils of birth and death, nor can you discern the root causes of parents, wives, children, brothers, and enemies within this world. Who is able to recognize their origin?

When you saw your son in the past, he was perhaps your enemy; if he had encountered suffering then, you would have rejoiced. Now that he is your son, you are distressed at his departure. Even if he were to die and be forcibly taken away, could you still give rise to anger toward me?
Have you not previously heard the words of the seers and sages:
"Whether young, middle-aged, or old, all return to death, just as fruit that has ripened naturally falls to the ground;
have you not observed that all birth and death is like the false visions experienced in a dream?"
Impermanence and the cycle of birth and death lead all sentient beings away; though they have parents, who can save them?
It is like a lion seizing and pouncing upon various deer; though those deer have mothers, even they cannot save them.
Old age, sickness, and death constantly harm sentient beings, just as a fruit tree is plucked by many people;
they are like earthenware vessels meeting falling rain, all of which rot and crumble away without remainder.
The sentient beings of the three realms are likewise; when they encounter the rain of impermanence, none can escape it.
Yet now they engage in these worldly activities and clearly create those future deeds; attached to pleasure, they do not observe or realize that death has arrived.
"Since these two children must inevitably be parted from me, I now give them away for the sake of the Dharma;
you should rejoice and not grieve. Although I am parting from my children, they will surely find peace and happiness; therefore, you should not give rise to great suffering."
After the Prince Bodhisattva had spoken these words, his wife remained silent and offered no further response.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra thought to himself:
"How extraordinary is this Bodhisattva!"
"Without any attachment or regret.
He then manifested a transformed body as a brahmin, went to where the Bodhisattva was, and spoke this verse:
"Great Seer, you should now know that your fame has reached the Brahma Heaven."
Capable of practicing great giving, And delighting in the True Dharma,
What I now seek and strive for Is hardly worth mentioning;
I only pray that the Great True Dharma May fulfill all my aspirations.
The Bodhisattva replied:

"I now regard my very body and life as entirely devoid of anything to cherish for myself; how much more so other external things, such as money, wealth, and precious jewels? Even if I possessed them, I would truly have no attachment to them."

"When I was formerly at home, I possessed many treasuries, elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, and servants; I gave them all in charity to the various brāhmaṇas, without any sense of lack or regret."
"But now, what is present here is empty and nothing exists; there is only myself and my wife. If you truly must have it, I truly do not begrudge it.
The Brahmin said, "If you can do this, then you may bestow your wife as a gift upon me."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I have long since abandoned envy and the mind of stinginess.
Listen for a moment while I preach the Dharma for her."
The Bodhisattva replied to his wife:
"This brahmin is begging you from me; what is your intention?
His wife then answered:
"Though you have full autonomy, I am now subject to you; how can I act according to my own will?
He then took his wife's hand and presented her to the brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:

"This woman now has a handsome countenance and a most exquisite form, her appearance being unsurpassed. The road ahead is perilous and infested with many bandits; as I am now alone, I will certainly not reach my destination. For now, let me entrust her to you; do not give her away to anyone else."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"I am now indebted to you for destroying my prison and severing my bonds; do you now wish to return me to that prison and bind me once more?"
The Brahmin said, "If you will have compassion for me and ensure that I obtain it, I pray that you accept it back for a brief moment.
Out of compassion, the Bodhisattva accepted it again for a short while; in the end, what suffering was there?
The brāhmaṇa said:
"If I should miss my appointed time and fail to return, you must take care not to give this away to anyone else; it is already mine, and you may not dispose of it as you please."
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
Not far from that place, he again manifested as another brahmin and returned to where the Bodhisattva was, saying:

"You bring supreme benefit to all sentient beings; you are like a fruit tree that constantly yields sweet fruit. From afar, I have long admired your reputation, and for this reason I have hurried here with uplifted robes to seek the fulfillment of your aspirations."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I have but one wife, whom I previously gave away to another; now I possess only this body, over which I still have full control, and if you require it, I shall provide it."
The brahmin said, “I have no need for your body;
I require only your two eyes. If you can grant them to me, I shall cherish this with the utmost sincerity.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This brahmin begs my eyes from me; what shall I do with them?
He further thought to himself:
"What am I to calculate?"
"This body is like a corpse in a cemetery; since it is not firm, one should joyfully exchange it for that which is firm.
What is there to worry about? At that time, the Bodhisattva took a khadira wood staff and made this vow:
"I now, for the sake of all sentient beings, cast away both my eyes without any greed or regret."
I have previously renounced my wife to bestow her upon others; may the merit of this act accrue to all sentient beings, so that they may forever sever their craving.
By the causal conditions of giving away my son, may they be freed from the habituation of attachment.
Now, by giving these two eyes, may all sentient beings attain the pure Dharma-eye.
After the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva had made this vow, he took a wooden awl and was about to gouge out his eye.
At that moment, a brāhmaṇa came forward and seized his hand, saying:
"Do not gouge it out! This eye now belongs to me; do not give it to anyone else."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I am but a single person now; how can I accept two trusts on one day?
A Brahmin has already entrusted my wife to me, and you now entrust your eyes to me. How could I possibly protect both?"
At that time, the brahmin immediately resumed his form as Śakra and said to the Bodhisattva, "Both my wife and my eyes are now yours; I entrust them to you. Do not give them away to anyone else."
At that time, Śakra immediately flew away and rained down four kinds of flowers from the midst of the sky. A voice resounded in the air, proclaiming to the devas:
"You should know that this person is nourishing the Bodhi tree; before long, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), their conduct is such that there is nothing they do not relinquish.
If all sentient beings were to hear of this matter, they should give rise to joy toward the bodhisattva in its entirety.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they act with a mind of ultimate concentration;
even Māra Pāpīyas cannot interrupt it.
I have heard this in the past:
In the past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha;
desiring to accomplish the path to Bodhi, he constantly practiced benefiting others and cultivated the True Dharma, harboring no thought of using weapons or staffs toward any sentient beings.

His countenance was upright and handsome, with few equals in the world; his speech was always accompanied by a smile, free from any coarseness or rudeness; he made offerings to his parents, revered his teachers and elders, and showed respect toward śramaṇas and renunciants.
He personally practices the ten wholesome deeds and also encourages others to do so; he constantly practices giving without interruption.

If there are those who are poor and distressed, their bodies emaciated and their clothing insufficient to cover them, the Bodhisattva, upon seeing them, immediately gives rise to compassion. His entire body trembles as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, and he thinks to himself:

"These sentient beings, due to the causes and conditions of stinginess and the ignorance of fools, do not recognize [the truth]; though they have received a human form with all its features complete, because they lack merit, they must constantly beg from others."
This is entirely due to their refusal to practice generosity in previous lives, having obscured themselves with stinginess and envy;
thus, as the retribution of the present life ripens, they undergo this suffering.

It is like a foolish and ignorant farmer who, having traveled a long distance to his wife’s family home and becoming hungry and thirsty on the road, enters her house only to find it empty. He immediately steals some non-glutinous rice, stuffing his mouth full and swallowing it whole. Before he has even swallowed it, the family members arrive; the man is filled with shame and cannot swallow it, yet out of regret, he does not spit it out.
When his family members saw him, they immediately asked,
"What ailment do you have that you are in such a state?
Having heard this, the man remained silent and said nothing.

At that time, the wife’s family members, both great and small, immediately summoned a skilled physician to treat him; seeing that his mouth and cheeks were as hard as wood or stone, they had no other recourse but to cut open the man's two cheeks with a knife.

After it was torn open, there was no pus or filth; instead, raw rice grains were seen filling his mouth. Because this person had concealed the act of theft, he received this visible retribution in the present life.
It is like a woman who conceals her pregnancy; when the day of delivery arrives, she undergoes great suffering and distress, crying out so loudly that everyone comes to know of it.

Human beings are likewise: when the retribution for their concealed transgressions ripens, they are compelled by suffering and exposed to the world; or, dwelling in a mind of stinginess, parsimony, and envy, they undergo this suffering.
I shall now block all paths so that stinginess and envy do not enter my mind; I shall now gather all that is to be given and establish all sentient beings within the practice of generosity.
At that time, after King Śūradatta had reflected on these matters, he constantly practiced giving without ceasing; while giving, his heart was filled with immeasurable joy.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān was filled with grief and distress, and he spoke these words:
"How strange! Śubhavyūha!"
"How is it that you have suddenly become my adversary and wish to analyze away my own realm?
I possess great power capable of subduing all sages—those who drink water, eat fruit, practice various austerities, and are skilled in accomplishing all mantra-arts."
"With a single shot of my flower-arrows, I can cause those who uphold the precepts to be utterly destroyed, just as the wind blows down and breaks great trees;
yet though I, Pāpīyān, have now shot three times, I fear I cannot cause the Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha’s body and mind to waver."

Why is this? Because the non-Buddhist seers lack wisdom and a heart of compassion; they do not seek to benefit others but act solely for their own pleasure. Therefore, upon being struck by the arrow, they immediately retreated and dispersed.

The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla possesses great wisdom and a profound heart of compassion; he seeks no personal pleasure but constantly acts for the sake of all beings. Although I have now shot three arrows, I still fear I may not be able to cause him to retreat or disperse.
Why is this? Because this person will certainly seek the unsurpassed path for the sake of all sentient beings and shall before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
While it has not yet been accomplished, I may, during that interval, create obstacles so as to cause it all to be destroyed.
It is like a person who has just fallen ill; if a physician provides a small amount of medicinal decoction, the illness can be cured.
It is also like a small tree: when it first sprouts, it can be severed with one's fingernails; but once it has grown large, even a hundred axes may find it difficult to fell.
Therefore, while this Bodhisattva has not yet perfected the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way, we must swiftly destroy him.
At that time, King Śubhavyūha, having practiced extensive acts of giving, sat alone in a quiet place to rest from his exhaustion.
Then, Pāpīyas appeared in the sky above, his body emitting a radiance that eclipsed the sun and moon, and spoke these words:
“Great King Śubhavyūha!
Excellent, excellent!
You are now truly able to seek the True Dharma and cherish sentient beings, just as a compassionate mother cherishes her child.
Well done, son of good family!

You wish to increase all wholesome dharmas, yet you instead inflame all unwholesome dharmas; it is like a person who wishes to eat ambrosia but eats poison, who seeks peace and happiness but enters among bandits, who desires a secure body but takes the wrong medicine, who wishes to eliminate thirst but drinks salt water, or who seeks to sever lustful desire but delights in a multitude of women.
"Good son! Do you not know?

There are donors who, due to the causes and conditions of their giving, all fall into hell. Therefore, out of compassion for you, I shall now analyze this in various ways for you to receive and uphold."
"From this day forward, you must sever the thought of giving and give rise to a mind of stinginess and attachment.
At that time, Pāpīyas immediately manifested hell-beings filling the entire place and showed them to Śubhavyūha, further saying:

"People such as these all practiced giving and greedily sought the True Dharma in previous lives; for this reason, they have today all fallen into this place to undergo great suffering and affliction."

"Great King, you should know that among these sinners, they merely hack and sever one another with knives and axes; though their limbs and joints all fall to the ground piece by piece, their lives still persist and they refuse to die.
Hot copper sheets are wrapped all around their bodies, and as smoke issues from their entire frames, their lives likewise do not end.
Although a thousand nails are driven through their bodies, they do not die, remaining like stretched ox-hide."
They run hither and thither, constantly encountering blazing fires and being tormented by various winds of cold and heat that press upon their bodies;

or there are fierce winds that blow their limbs apart, or they are beaten with clubs until they are reduced to dust; they swallow iron balls when hungry and drink molten copper when thirsty; or they enter forests of knives and climb trees of swords; or they are placed in great cauldrons, rising and falling with the boiling water until they are as decomposed as cooked beans.
Although these sentient beings undergo such various sufferings and afflictions, their life-faculties nevertheless refuse to perish.

Great King, you should know that I now seek nothing from the King, nor do I seek any articles of worship; rather, because the King practices a deviant and heterodox path, I have come here today to expound the True Path for him.
At that time, King Śubhavyūha, seeing such beings within the hells, immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion and thought to himself:

"These beings wander through birth and death with no prospect of escape; having already endured immeasurable and manifold sufferings, they now once again undergo torment in this hell—how pitiable and how tragic!"
"When shall I attain the severance of all suffering and affliction so that none remain?
Thus, these sentient beings previously practiced unwholesome dharmas and now undergo the retribution of suffering; they receive what they themselves have created, which is truly not my suffering."

I now know for certain that these immeasurable sentient beings who undergo suffering all did so because they committed many unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind in previous lives; it is for this reason that they have fallen into these states of retribution today, and it is certainly not because of giving that they suffer.
At that time, King Śubhavyūha, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward Pāpīyas, spoke these words: "Excellent,
O Great Being!"

"You are truly compassionate and possess a heart of mercy; you skillfully explain the characteristics of the path and the non-path. If it causes the donor to undergo such suffering, where then would those who receive the gift be?"
Pāpīyān replied: "Excellent,
O Bodhisattva!"
You possess profound wisdom to be able to inquire about this meaning.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain this for you.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, by means of his own supernatural power, immediately manifested the physical forms of various devas; he adorned his body with celestial necklaces, jeweled garlands, flowers, and incense;
he provided himself with the entertainment of immeasurable musical performances, and was attended on all sides by celestial maidens.
Various kinds of trees constantly produce sweet fruits; trees of flowers, necklaces, garments, food, drink, and so forth stand arrayed before one.
Immeasurable flocks of birds sing in harmony, their voices melodious and refined, most delightful to hear.
Everywhere there are many flowing springs and bathing pools, with golden lotuses spread across the water's surface.
There is no sound of the sufferings of old age, sickness, or death, and his body dwells within a subtle palace made of the seven treasures.
Having transformed it thus, Māra immediately showed it to the Bodhisattva, saying:
“O son of good family!

All those who receive these gifts shall likewise experience immeasurable supreme bliss; therefore, you should now relinquish your stinginess and practice giving, for from this point forward you shall be able to receive such subtle and wondrous karmic rewards.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"Such words are inverted and false; they possess no logical consistency. Why is this so?"
I have never seen a harītakī tree produce sugarcane;
nor have I seen pure lotuses emerge from excrement and filth;
nor have I seen pure, wondrous gold transform into copper or iron.
"That a donor with faith should undergo the sufferings of hell—such words cause great harm; these words are perverse and are certainly the speech of Māra.
He then spoke as follows:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully distinguished such merits; you have already taken me into your grasp.
He then spoke again to Māra:
"You should now know this: just as the wind-force from the wings of a locust cannot blow and move Sumeru, the King of Mountains, so too is it with your desire to move me by means of your wind-force."
As previously stated, it would truly accord with my wish if those donors, by reason of their giving, were to fall into hell, while those who receive the gifts were born in the heavens.
"I vow that from this day forth, may I alone be the donor and constantly fall into the hells, while causing all sentient beings to become the recipients [of my merit] and be born in the heavens.
To undergo suffering in a single body so that many may enjoy happiness—is this not the fundamental vow of a Bodhisattva?"

"I now know for certain that you are Pāpīyān; you shall not be able to engage me in battle. Since time immemorial, I have constantly cultivated a mind of generosity; how can you now suddenly cause me to abandon it?"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) in this manner, even the celestial Māras cannot obstruct them.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the unsurpassed path for the sake of all sentient beings,
they even sacrifice their heads and eyes.
I have heard that in the past,
in this kingdom of Kāśī, there was a king named Candraprabha;
he cultivated the path to enlightenment and, seeking the benefit of the Dharma, constantly censured all sensual desires.

That king’s physical form was upright, dignified, and beautiful; his wisdom and talent surpassed others, being rarely equaled in the world. He was honest and straightforward, free from flattery; his speech was gentle, and he was profoundly sincere without deception. He remained far removed from anger, and all shared in harmony and joy.

He reveres śramaṇas and brahmins; he is compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient, making offerings to his parents. The kings of neighboring kingdoms submit to his virtue and respect him, bowing from afar and honoring him as a friend. His fame and virtue spread throughout all directions, and he is constantly able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
He protects all the people within his realm, just as a compassionate mother loves her own infant; furthermore, at a later time, he secretly gives rise to this thought:
"By what means shall I cause the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice?"
He immediately summoned his great ministers and spoke these words:

"You all must now adorn this city, hanging flowered canopies, erecting precious banners and streamers, sweeping and sprinkling the streets, burning incense, and scattering flowers upon the ground, so that the people shall have no sorrow or suffering.
Let them all adorn their bodies with precious necklaces and garlands, and let their clothing and ornaments be made as bright and radiant as possible."
The ministers knelt and assented, respectfully receiving the king’s command. They immediately went out and proclaimed it to all the people of the city:
"Each of you must adorn the city walls and gates, and ensure that every street and alleyway is made utterly pure, so that it resembles the palaces of the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
At that time, King Candraprabha mounted a great elephant and departed from the palace, whereupon he commanded an official:
"Go, convey my words to the people:
'I have now adorned this city and its walls not out of greed, arrogance, pride, or fear of enemies; nor do I seek to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
The reason I now adorn this city is solely to enable all sentient beings to experience immeasurable happiness and not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
"You all should today regard me as your parents, brothers, and spiritual friends.
If you enter my palace, it shall be as if it were your own home; take whatever you require according to your own will.
I am now performing this great act of giving, so do not harbor doubts or hesitation. After taking these things, you should practice wholesome dharmas."

Beyond what is required for my own sustenance, I shall further bestow it upon others; even if they should desire my body or life, I would not begrudge them, wishing only that all may receive peace and happiness.

When King Candraprabha had spoken these words, he had all the exquisite treasures within his palace carried out by servants to be distributed as alms according to their wishes. He regarded all the people as if they were his own parents, brothers, or infants, his countenance serene and joyful like the autumn moon.
All the people looked up to this king as they would to a father, a mother, an elder brother, or a younger brother; with virtuous hearts, they gazed upon the king as if his eyes were blue lotuses.

At that time, there were no people in the kingdom who carried swords or staves; all followed the king in practicing the ten wholesome deeds, just as oxen follow a bull-king, or as the myriad stars follow the moon;
like a multitude of merchants following behind their leader, or like a host of soldiers following their general.
For example, because the seeds of the grape are sweet, the fruit that grows from them is also sweet;
as with the sandalwood tree, both its roots and its flowers are fragrant.
It was likewise with King Candraprabha, who caused all the people to practice the ten wholesome paths of action.

At that time, there was not even a single person in that country who harbored anger or envy, pride or arrogance, haughtiness or stubbornness; nor did anyone steal another's wealth, violate another's wife, engage in double-tongued speech or harsh words, or hold greed, malice, or false views.

Although King Candraprabha was not a sage-king, his subjects all practiced the ten wholesome deeds. At that time, although the people lacked clothing made of grass or food consisting of fruits and gourds, their physical appearance was no different from that of the immortals; they all craved the deep mountains and secluded places, yet because of their love for the king, they were unable to leave him.
When the king had thus practiced the wholesome Dharma, various śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others proclaimed his virtue, so that its fame spread throughout all directions.
At that time, there was an elderly brāhmaṇa who had renounced domestic life and sensual desires, dwelling in the Snowy Mountains;
with long hair, beard, and nails as the marks of his holy life, he used a mat of woven grass for clothing and fruit and water to ward off hunger.
Having heard it said that King Candraprabha was fond of giving and free from stinginess,
he recalled his former habits upon hearing these words, and immediately gave rise to an evil thought.
It is like casting oil into a fierce fire; once the oil has reached it, the fire blazes all the more intensely.

It is also like administering poison into fresh blood, whereby its potency becomes even more powerful. It is like a thirsty person drinking salt water, or like the increase of heat in autumn and the abundance of mucus and spittle in spring.
This Brahmin, dwelling in the deep mountains, heard of the King’s meritorious virtues and his anger increased accordingly;
it was just like a sleeping lion hearing the sound of deer—that Brahmin’s anger grew in the same way.
He further thought:
"All the world is utterly deluded and devoid of wisdom, having been deceived and confused by this king."
"I shall now go and seek one thing, to ascertain whether this king is truly able to renounce it.
He further thought:
"If no one were to beg for my very life, I might still be swayed; but if there is someone who asks for it, I will certainly turn back from my resolve."

Having formed this thought, he immediately emerged from the deep mountains, abandoned the pure Dharma, and his anger increased; his mouth became like red copper, his lips were pressed together with gritted teeth, and he brandished his limbs with his jaws wide open.

It is like a malevolent dragon releasing hail to destroy grain; like a vajra-pestle shattering a great mountain; like an asura king obstructing and seizing the sun and moon; like torrential rain flooding and submerging villages; and like a fierce, blazing fire consuming dry grass.
This brahmin was likewise; harboring such an evil mind, he went to King Candraprabha in the city of Kāśī.
He manifested these signs of his habitual wickedness: his body trembled, his speech was stammering, and his gait was not straight upon the path.

His hands were curled and twisted; his eyebrows and whiskers were swift and fierce; his hair stood on end; his five fingers, covered by his palms, resembled five dragon heads; within his heart, poison surged like a venomous serpent; and from his breath of rage, a dense smoke and flames rose together as he spoke deceitfully:
"Great King!"
While I was on the Snowy Mountains, I heard your name from afar and rejoiced with immeasurable exultation.
I have observed that among all kings there is none like you; this land possesses incalculable merit, and you have further encountered such a Dharma King.

"Great King, for the sake of benefiting others today, you ought to sacrifice your own life; those who practice the True Dharma sleep and wake in constant peace. I now wish to request one thing of the Great King."
The king immediately replied, "Great Brahmin, there is no need for many words;

please command what must be done. Whatever you require shall be provided in full: whether elephants, horses, chariots, oxen, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, clothing, precious gems, or male and female slaves and attendants—all shall be granted to you."

"Brahmin! You should now know that these sentient beings are tormented by the three poisons and wander through birth and death with no time of liberation. The laws of old age, sickness, and death constantly afflict them; I alone am able to transcend them, yet I remain in this world for a long time solely for the sake of sentient beings. Whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."
The brahmin said,
"If Your Majesty can do so, you must first fix your mind and not allow it to waver.
The king then replied:

"Since ancient times, I have constantly established vows such that my mind is difficult to move; for the sake of sentient beings, I have resolved upon bodhicitta, and I would even sacrifice my own body and life, let alone other external things."

You should now know this: if one possesses wealth and property yet is unable to practice giving, you should know that such a person is merely a slave guarding their master's goods. They are like a poisonous tree that, though it produces flowers and fruit, yields nothing for anyone to enjoy; or like a deep well with a short rope where water cannot be reached—possessing wealth but not practicing giving is exactly like this.
If, upon seeing a beggar, one’s face contorts with a frown, you should know that such a person has opened the gate to the realm of hungry ghosts.
The brahmin said: "Excellent,
Great King!"
"What benefit is there in these empty words? If you can truly do so, then offer your head as a gift.
When the ministers heard these words, they said to the Brahmin, "How strange!
You are a great thief!"
"From where have you come?
You have uttered meaningless words with your mouth!
Thereupon, they vied with one another to strike and bespatter him with earth and stones, and together they cried out:
"Such a person as this is not a brāhmaṇa; how could there be one who wears grass and deerskin, has long hair, observes dietary restrictions, and yet utters such thorny words?"

Though their bodies and attire resemble those of sages and saints, the words they utter are worse than those of a caṇḍāla; since their physical conduct and speech do not correspond with one another, you should know for certain that they are not brāhmaṇas, but rather rākṣasas and malevolent spirits.
"Alas, you wicked man!
Have you come here now wishing to dry up our river of the True Dharma?
Do you wish to devour the Dharma-dragons like a garuḍa, thereby cutting off the rain of the Dharma?"

You are like a malignant wind that extinguishes the torch of the Dharma; you are a great evil elephant wishing to uproot the tree of the Dharma. You are a person of deathly wickedness who lacks all principle.
When you speak words from your mouth, why does your tongue not shrink back?
"How is it that the great earth can support your body?
How is it that the blazing heat of the sun does not scorch your body, and how is it that those rivers do not sweep you away?
At that time, the brāhmaṇa said to the ministers:
"You foolish people, why do you revile me?
It is like a vicious dog barking at a beggar; do you now suspect that I am not a brāhmaṇa coming from afar to seek alms?"
Is this not an ordained monk of vast learning?
You fools and evildoers cannot even perceive the power possessed by these brahmins; do you not know this?

The waning and waxing of the sun and moon, the saltiness and bitterness of the great ocean, the seer Śaṇu drinking the Gaṅgā until it ceased to flow for twelve years, the three eyes on the face of the sovereign King of Gods,

the seer Gautama transforming a thousand female organs upon the body of Śakra, the seer Vasiṣṭha transforming Śakra’s body into the form of a ram, and the great seer Viśvāmitra eating Mount Sumeru as if it were a bowl of milk porridge— all such matters are entirely due to the power of us Brahmins.

I have come here now not merely for the sake of your empty words and flowery embellishments; for who among kings, when claiming to themselves that they can give all things, would be subject to reproach if I were to beg from them now?
At that time, King Candraprabha spoke to his ministers:
"You should not obstruct me now; I shall cause this Brahmin’s wish to be fulfilled."

"You should observe this: I now govern the kingdom free from greed, hatred, and delusion; the karmic fruit I have attained is now fully realized, and the time has come for me to cast off this body, just as a snake sheds its skin."
"You should know this: I shall now exchange this non-durable body for that durable body; trade this non-durable wealth for durable wealth; and exchange this non-durable life for a durable life."
As I have often taught you the Dharma of the Great Man in the past, now is precisely the time for it;

I have also constantly exhorted you to turn toward the True Dharma, to close off all evils and open the gates of all virtues, to plant various roots of goodness within Bodhi, to attenuate the afflictions, and gradually untie the bonds of the household. Just as I have attained these merits, you too shall attain them.

Therefore, I now relinquish my body and life; you should rejoice and not feel sorrow or distress. Even if I had clung to this body and been unable to act, I would still have used harsh words to comfort and exhort you until you did so.

How much more so today, when I am able to cut through my own [delusions] by myself, yet you instead obstruct and firmly refuse to allow it—like a person who would trade grass for wool, or seek to cure an illness with poison.
"I am likewise; having abandoned this non-durable body, I shall obtain a durable body.
At that time, the ministers spoke again, saying:
"Your Majesty should not expect to obtain a durable body by calculating such matters as these."
Then the ministers spoke again, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should not dwell upon this matter.
Why is that? For what reason?"
"Your Majesty is the one upon whom we rely; this body of yours is now shared by all of us. How can you wish to abandon this shared thing for the sake of a single Brahmin alone?"
Once this body has been cast aside, how can the matter of giving wealth be accomplished?
If it cannot be accomplished, those who suffer will be many.
Although the king’s person is shared by the whole world, why do you alone today desire to exercise sovereign power?
"It is like a magnificent jewel shared by many people; if one person uses it alone, can they truly exercise mastery over it?
Your Majesty’s body is now just like this.
At that time, the Great King, with a serene countenance and a joyful expression, spoke again to his ministers:
"You should first arouse a heart of compassion and regard this brāhmaṇa; only then shall I give up my head to him.
At that time, the Great King said to the brāhmaṇa:
"Step aside for a moment, so that I may console my ministers and subjects; once I have done so, I shall send you on your way."
At that time, the brahmin stepped back a short distance.
Then, the Great King addressed his ministers, saying:
"Do you not know my original vow, which has always been to benefit all sentient beings?"
"I have already accomplished what was to be done for you, yet I shall further fulfill this Brahmin's wish.

This Brahmin once harbored enmity toward me in the past; as the karmic retribution remains unfinished, he constantly dwells upon it in his mind. Since there is no other means by which I may repay him, I must relinquish my head so that the debt may be forever settled."
"Since I have received this body, I have always practiced the True Dharma; now, for the sake of this person as well, I shall practice the True Dharma.
You all, depart quickly!
Having thus addressed them, he summoned the brāhmaṇa and sent him back to his own place, speaking these words:
"You lack skillful wisdom and do not know the proper timing; why do you seek my head in the midst of this great assembly instead of seeking it in a secluded place?"
I now exhort and advise your ministers on your behalf so that you may remain secure and preserve your life;
had they not been exhorted, how could your body and life have been fully saved?
"Go a short distance away to a secluded place; once I have dismissed my ministers, I shall come to you and grant you the gift of my own head.
When the brāhmaṇa heard the king's words, he immediately departed to a distant location.
At that time, after the Great King had dispatched his ministers, he went to the brahmin himself and said to him:
"If you have now been sent by my enemy to seek my head, I harbor no feelings of enmity or resentment toward you."
If you come here to demand [recompense] yourself, for what reason? You, O Brahmin, should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness;

if you give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, you shall immediately be reborn in heaven. Let your heart of enmity be extinguished quickly, for it is like fire. When hatred dwells in the heart, one does not perceive the meaning of the Dharma. One who cultivates patience eliminates hatred; hatred defiles the mind so that the form is no longer upright, just as clouds and mist obscure the pure moon.
"One who has left the household life should not give rise to such things; one who gives rise to anger will not be upright and handsome, just as one who drinks alcohol emits foul and stinking breath.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Although what you have now said is wonderful and excellent, how could I, being coarse and unruly, be able to believe and accept it?"
"I simply say, 'Give me my head,' and no more.
Although what you have said is well-intentioned, hearing it only serves to increase my anger even further, like pouring oil onto a raging fire."

Then the king replied, "Since my birth, I have never encouraged anyone to commit an evil deed. As for this body, you may cut it as you wish; this body is loathsome like a pit of filth and is truly not dear to me. I do so only out of compassion for you, lest you fall into hell."
The brāhmaṇa asked,
"Where is this so-called hell located?
At that moment, the great king immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion and spoke these words:
"How strange are sentient beings!
How lamentable is this world!
For there is not a single person who practices wholesome dharmas for their own benefit."

Although I have exhorted and admonished this man in various ways, his fundamental mind still delights in committing evil. It is like a fly inside a vessel of honey; even when someone pulls it out, its heart still clings to the sweetness, and because of that attachment, it even loses its life. This brāhmaṇa is just like that.

At that time, the brahmin took a sharp blade, covered it with a deer skin, and then drew it forth; he seized the king by the hair and bound him to a tree, intending with a mind of fierce hatred to sever the king's head.
The blade missed its mark and instead severed a tree branch;

at that moment, the Brahmin, thinking he had already struck his victim, was filled with joy. However, due to the majestic power of the Bodhisattva and the various celestial deities, he could not even see the king’s head or body.
At that time, the tree deity said to the brahmin:
"How could there be such a person claiming to be a brahmin who keeps a sharp sword and takes the lives of others? Why do your hands not fall to the ground?"
"Why did the earth not split open and swallow you?
Why did you give rise to such an evil thought toward this pure person?
That your body did not sink into the earth was due to the protection afforded by this Bodhisattva."

At that time, the brahmin, believing he had truly severed the Bodhisattva’s head, felt his resentment dissolve and immediately departed; the king also returned to his palace, his body safe and unharmed.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the *dānapāramitā*, they are able to act in such a way that there is nothing they do not relinquish.
*Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhānasūtra*, Middle Scroll;
*Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhānasūtra*, Lower Scroll.
Compiled by Saṃghasena;
translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva falls into the realm of animals,
The various wholesome dharmas he practices cannot be matched by non-Buddhists.
As I have heard:

In the past, when the Bodhisattva was once in the form of a hare, although he had received the body of a hare due to the causal conditions of residual karma from previous lives, he was skilled in human speech; his words were always sincere and free from falsehood.
Having achieved wisdom, they remain far removed from anger and are foremost among gods and humans;
with compassion perfuming their hearts, they are harmonious, gentle, and kind, able to utterly extinguish all conditions for Māra;
their words and deeds correspond, they are truthful and free from flattery, and the intent to harm shall never arise again.
Abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru, he was the leader of immeasurable rabbits and constantly spoke these words to all the rabbits:
"Do you not know that you will fall into the evil realms!"
This body is fraught with affliction.

As for the evil realms—namely, the hells, the animals, the hungry ghosts, and the asuras—these are what are called the evil realms. You should now listen with a sincere mind to the causes and conditions for falling into these evil realms, which are known as the ten non-virtuous actions.
"In the past, I heard various sages analyze and explain this, and I have also reflected upon it with my own mind; I shall now briefly explain it for you.
The four roots of phenomena bring many afflictions: namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and pride."
Those who commit the ten non-virtues out of a mind of greed fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
those who commit the ten non-virtues out of a mind of hatred fall into the realm of animals;
and those who commit the ten non-virtues out of a mind of delusion fall into hell.

Those who commit the ten unwholesome deeds out of a mind of arrogance fall among the asuras; by virtue of these four factors, they go to places where they constantly experience suffering and affliction.

"You all should observe that within the hells there are fierce fires blazing and sharp knives used for flaying and skinning; one is constantly devoured by dogs and jackals, while iron-beaked crows peck and gouge out one's eyes. The Ash River destroys the body until it is like fine dust, and one is further smashed by various hammers. Sharp axes, blades, and swords sever one's hands and feet, while cold, evil winds blow and wrinkle one's body."
"Two mountains strike one another with the bodies of beings situated between them.

You should know that even if I were to spend my entire lifespan throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes explaining such hells, I could not exhaustively describe the various sufferings of the sentient beings in these hells."

"You should now further listen to the various sufferings within the realm of hungry ghosts: namely, being tormented by hunger and thirst, their bodies withered and parched, and for immeasurable years having never even heard the names of liquids or water."

Even when seeking it, I could not find anything but foul excrement; my hair was long and sharp, entangling my body and causing the fires within my limbs and joints to blaze. From afar I saw water, but upon reaching it, it became a pit of fire. Driven by hunger and thirst, I went toward the filth, only to be firmly obstructed by evil spirits bearing swords and staves. To speak of this now redoubles the terror and dread in my heart.

"As for the asuras, although they enjoy the five desires no differently than the devas, they are arrogant and self-exalting, lacking a humble mind. They distance themselves from spiritual friends and do not believe in the Triple Gem; furthermore, they are not protected by virtuous companions. Within this world, they give rise to perverted views; though they see the Buddhas, their hearts lack reverence and faith. Toward the higher devas, they constantly harbor evil intentions, fixating their thoughts on seeking out the faults of those devas."
You should all know that the fetter of pride and arrogance entails many faults and provides no benefit.

That sentient beings fail to attain the fruits of the Path is entirely due to this flourishing arrogance, whereby they assert their own views as right while disparaging and reviling others. Because of such arrogance, worldly beings increase in false views; through the conditions of these false views, they slander the Triple Gem.

Because they slander the Triple Gem, they are reborn as asuras; the various sufferings experienced among the asuras could not be fully described even if one were to attempt to do so for the sake of others.

Due to the causes and conditions of ignorance, they fall among the animals and undergo manifold sufferings, assuming various forms, eating various foods, and speaking various languages with differing modes of conduct and dwelling.

Those without feet, those with two feet, those with four feet, and those with many feet; those that move in water, on land, or through the air—such as oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, pigs, swine, chickens, dogs, flying birds, and running beasts—all such beings are constantly shrouded and obscured by ignorance.

Constantly dwelling in blindness and darkness, they lack wisdom; each harbors thoughts of killing toward the other, fearing one another as if they were enemies or bandits. They are constantly slain by hunters, butchers, and meat-carvers, and are further torn apart and devoured by lions, tigers, wolves, jackals, dogs, and countless other evil beasts.

They constantly fall into pits, ditches, ravines, and nets of thorns; while alive they carry heavy burdens, and at death they are flayed and skinned, yoked to plows and pulled by carts with iron hooks piercing their noses, bound by leather straps and tethered.
They are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst; their mouths are parched and their tongues dry, yet though they have needs, they cannot express them with their mouths.

Young, orphaned, and scattered abroad, they are far removed from their parents. Though water and grass are boundless, they are never sufficient. Such is the evil retribution of animals, clearly visible in this world; therefore, I shall now briefly explain this for you all.

"Because of the evil causes and conditions of my past karma, I have received this body of a rabbit; I subsist only on water and grass and am constantly beset by great fear. Therefore, you all should cultivate wholesome dharmas. Through the causes and conditions of wholesome dharmas, one is born among gods or humans. Although there are various sufferings and afflictions in the human realm that exceed those of the gods, you should nevertheless make a vow to be born among humans."
For example, according to the laws of the state, earthen pits are constructed for those who have committed crimes, consisting of three levels:
those who have committed grave offenses are placed at the bottom;
those who have committed middling offenses are placed in the middle; and so forth.
Those whose offenses are extremely light are placed at the top of the heavy ones.

It is the same for those who perform evil deeds: those with the most grievous evils fall into hell; those with middling evils receive the bodies of animals; and those of the lowest grade are born among the hungry ghosts.
Having distanced themselves from these three types of evil, they are reborn among human beings; once reborn as humans, they practice both wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
Those who practice supreme goodness enter nirvana as if entering their own home.
At that time, the hare-king constantly preached such virtuous and sublime words to all the hares.
Now, there was a man of the Brahmin caste who, weary of the world, left the household life to practice the dharma of a seer;

he did not afflict living beings, had abandoned desire and attachment, spoke with a gentle countenance, and his body was free from coarseness. He drank water and ate fruits and various medicinal roots.
With few desires and contentment, he practiced the conduct of tranquility, allowing his hair and nails to grow long as a sign of his holy life (*brahmacarya*).
At that time, the seer suddenly heard from afar the king of the rabbits preaching the Dharma to the rabbits; having heard this, he felt remorse in his heart and spoke these words:
"Although I have now been born among human beings, I am foolish and ignorant, unlike this rabbit who, though born among rabbits, clearly understands the wholesome Dharma."
Just as the light of the sun obscures the light of the moon, so it is with me.

Although I am born among humans, I am obscured by those who are like animals; yet though they are like animals, some may be upholders of the True Dharma, or even Brahmā Kings or Maheśvaras. Now that I have heard the Dharma they preach, my mind becomes harmonious and gentle, just as a person overcome by heat enters cool, clear water.
"How strange, O Lion!
Having committed many evil deeds, you have received this animal body; how could you possibly kill such a rabbit?

This rabbit is one of pure goodness; though its form is such, it is able to practice the dharma of sages and saints. Though born as a beast, it is capable of proclaiming the characteristics of good and evil."
"From time immemorial, I have had no one to consult or revere; that I have now encountered such a person is a source of immeasurable goodness.
At that moment, the rishi rose, joined his palms in reverence, and went to where the hare was.
Having arrived at the rabbit’s dwelling, he withdrew to sit to one side; joining his palms toward the rabbit, he spoke these words:
“You are the embodiment of the True Dharma; you shall not undergo rebirth as a rabbit. Whatever purely wholesome dharmas you possess, I pray that you will explain them fully for my sake.”

The practices I have cultivated—growing out my beard and hair, wearing robes of grass, and eating fruit—I now truly find wearying; it is like seeking ghee by churning ice, which is truly difficult to obtain, and I am just like that.
"Though one may grow long hair, wear garments of grass, and subsist on fruit throughout one's life, even if one practices such asceticism, the True Dharma is difficult to attain.

Although I have now been born among humans and possess a human form, I am far removed from spiritual friends and practice unwholesome dharmas. Just as the saptaparṇa flower is fit only to be viewed from afar and not to be approached closely, so too am I."
"A wise person regards one who practices evil dharmas as someone to be shunned from afar and will never draw near them; you are truly a Brahmā King who has merely assumed the body of a rabbit.
The rabbit then replied:
"Great Brāhmaṇa!"
If what I have said does not please your mind, it is because you do not love it greatly. Why is this?
It is because I have long since abandoned the fetter of stinginess.

"In the past, when you first resolved to attain enlightenment, you should have entered nirvana immediately; it is only for the sake of sentient beings that you remain long in the cycle of birth and death.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin felt great joy in his heart and said:
"You are a Great Being, capable of dwelling long within this world for the sake of sentient beings."
He followed him for many years, drinking water and eating fruit no differently than the rabbit.

At that time, the people of the world practiced many unwholesome dharmas; because of these causes and conditions, the heavens suffered a severe drought. Grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits withered and failed to emerge; the waters of the oceans, ponds, wells, and springs dried up and vanished. All the timber, brush, weeds, and grasses upon the land were gathered and carried away by the people.
At that time, the brahmin, emaciated by hunger and suffering from great distress, addressed the hare with a gentle countenance, saying:
"I wish now to depart; I pray you do not reproach me."
Having heard this, the hare immediately thought to himself, "This great seer does not delight in this place; that is why he wishes to abandon me.
He then stepped forward and asked:
"What fault is there here? What offense has been committed?

Great Seer, you should consider that it is inappropriate for your mind to be filled with such grief and distress while wearing these robes of *kuśa* grass; it is as improper as a Brahmin entering the house of a courtesan."
The Brahmin said:
"What you have spoken truly enters my heart; this place is pure and truly free from harm, for the rabbits cultivate themselves here and do not trespass upon one another."
However, I am of meager merit and exhausted by lack of food and drink; for this reason, I must reluctantly bid you farewell.

You should now observe that all sentient beings sustain their bodies without exception through food. Although we must now part from these excellent and sublime Dharma essentials you have spoken, we shall surely wear them upon our hearts for the rest of our lives, never allowing them to be forgotten.
"You should further know that my heart is devoid of compassion; for the sake of foul food, I wish to abandon you and depart.
At that time, the hare replied, "What you have done is but a minor matter; why then do you wish to abandon me and go?"
The brahmin said:
"I have been drinking nothing but water for many days; fearing that my life may not be preserved, I wish to abandon you."
Having heard this, the hare thought to himself:
"Excellent! This brahmin is truly capable of drinking nothing but water for many days for the sake of the Dharma."
He then said: "If you depart, I shall have no such field of merit; I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will graciously accept my invitation."
Although one knows that a bodhisattva has no discrimination in their mind regarding the field of merit, the merit is greatest when giving to sentient beings suffering from extreme hunger and thirst;
although one knows that both eyes are always to be protected, one should first rescue the part that is in pain.
"You are now my close spiritual friend; you are one whom I revere and who possesses great merit. Therefore, I now wish to provide a modest offering.
You should know that there are four types of people, and likewise four types of giving:
namely, the inferior, the inferior-middle-inferior, the wise, and the wise-middle-wise."
What is the inferior [giving]?
It is when, at the time of giving, one generates the aspiration to seek existence within the realms of becoming (*bhava*).
What is the most inferior of the inferior?
One practices giving out of fear;
the wise person practices giving with a mind of reverence.
"Among those who possess wisdom, the wisest are those who practice giving with a heart of great compassion.
Of these four kinds of giving, I now intend to practice one; I only pray that you will surely accept my invitation tomorrow morning."
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"What has this rabbit seen today?
Has it seen a dead deer?"
"Or perhaps it is a dead rabbit?
His heart was immediately filled with joy; he lit a fire and recited mantras.
That night, the rabbit gathered a great deal of dry wood and addressed the other rabbits, saying:
"You should know this: this brahmin now wishes to abandon me and go far away to another's house; I am deeply distressed, and my body trembles.

Such is the nature of worldly phenomena—impermanent and subject to separation, empty, false, and unreal like a magical illusion. Union is followed by separation, just like the autumn rains. Conditioned things possess such immeasurable faults and afflictions; all conditioned formations are like dreams or mirages in the heat. When the life of sentient beings is exhausted, there is no returning."
"You all now know that the nature of worldly phenomena is thus, yet you are unable to leave it behind; therefore, you must diligently strive to destroy the three realms of existence!
At that time, the rabbit king did not sleep throughout the entire night, preaching the Dharma to the assembly of rabbits in this manner.
When the night had ended, at the clear dawn, he went to the side of the pile of firewood and blew upon the fire. Once the fire was ignited, he spoke to the brāhmaṇa, saying:
"Yesterday I invited you, wishing to provide a modest offering; it is now fully prepared. I pray that you will certainly partake of it."
Why is this? When a wise person gathers wealth with the intent to practice giving, the recipient, out of compassion, will certainly accept and utilize it;
however, if an ordinary person were to amass great treasures and give them away to others, that would not be considered difficult.
I am now poor, and thus it is difficult for me to give; I only pray that you will have compassion and accept this for certain.
I now entreat you with a deeply pure heart; I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will accept it without hesitation.
Having spoken these words, he further consoled himself:
"Now, for the sake of bestowing peace and happiness upon others, I shall sacrifice my own body without begrudging or clinging to it even as much as a single hair."
"By this merit, may all sentient beings realize unsurpassed wisdom.
Having thus comforted himself, he threw himself into the fire pit.
At that time, the brahmin, seeing this, was struck with terror and his hair stood on end; he immediately pulled him out from atop the flames.
His impermanent life was suddenly cut short; with his heart overwhelmed by grief, he took the body onto his lap, gazed at it, and wept aloud, saying:
"O lover of the Dharma, Great Sage of Compassion, Tamer and Master of the Ship!"
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, you sacrificed your body and life; where have you gone now?
I now pay homage to you as my Lord of Refuge.
Dwelling on this mountain with this heavy burden of long hair, though many years have passed, it has brought me no benefit.
"I vow from this day forth to always carry you upon my head; may your merits be fully accomplished, and may I always be your disciple in future lives.

Having spoken these words, he returned to his rabbit body, set it down on the ground, and prostrated himself with his head at its feet. He then took it up again as if it were a newborn infant, and together with the dead rabbit, he threw himself into the fire pit.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having learned of these matters, made grand offerings and collected the bones to erect a stūpa.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing such perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) does not deceive the world.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the great pāramitās,
never gives rise to an evil mind even toward his greatest enemies.
I have heard this in the past:
In a past life, the Bodhisattva fell among the animals and took the body of a deer;
his two flanks were golden in color and his spine resembled lapis lazuli, while the rest of his body was a variegated mixture of colors so diverse that it was difficult to name them.
His hooves were like *śukti* (mother-of-pearl), his horns like refined gold, and his body was as magnificent as a treasury of the seven precious jewels.
He constantly acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, fully accomplishing all wholesome dharmas.
His physical radiance was like the sun first rising, and because the devas revered him, they bestowed upon him the name "Golden Deer."

He acts as a leader for immeasurable deer; this king of deer practices great compassion, and is fully endowed with diligence and wisdom without deficiency. Possessing great courage and bravery, he understands human speech well, having manifested the body of a deer to harmonize and guide sentient beings.

At that time, the Deer King roamed the Snowy Mountains, which abounded in groves, flowers, fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools. Whenever various birds and beasts harbored mutual animosity or gave rise to thoughts of robbery and harm, they were all entirely extinguished by the power of this Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, leaving nothing behind.
In that secluded and tranquil place, he constantly instructed the deer, teaching them to distance themselves from all evils and practice wholesome dharmas. He addressed the deer, saying:
"Listen, all of you!
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you should regard even a minor evil as being like poisoned food; such minor evils must not be accepted."
You should regard even small virtues as dear friends; you should constantly draw near to them and diligently uphold them.

Because you deer have committed various evils through body, speech, and mind, you have fallen among the animals and are unable to practice any wholesome dharmas. Shrouded by ignorance, you have received these animal bodies and will find it difficult to escape from the midst of birth and death throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
Those who wish to experience happiness must take the True Dharma as their foundation. Indeed, the True Dharma can protect sentient beings from falling into the evil realms.

It serves as a bridge for those seeking to cross the ocean of the suffering of afflictions; it is like a person in a perilous place relying on a stool or a staff, or like one holding a torch to clearly see various vessels.
It is the same for those who practice the True Dharma; indeed, the True Dharma is most worthy of being approached and cannot be destroyed, for it can show sentient beings the unsurpassed Great Way.

This is that which enables those who experience pleasure; having heard this Dharma, it can cause the mind to rejoice. For one whose mind and mind-state proceed uninterruptedly in accordance with this Dharma, the mind has nothing to fear; this Dharma is able to eliminate all evils.

Just as excellent medicine cures all manner of illnesses, for this reason one should always maintain mindfulness of it and not allow it to be forgotten; if it is forgotten, this life will pass in vain, for all that exists in the world is entirely deceptive.
Only the dharmas of generosity, patience, shame, and wisdom are truly real; if one can practice such dharmas as these, this is called being fully endowed with the True Dharma.
For the sake of the birds and beasts, he constantly preached this Dharma, causing those who listened to have their minds free from lustful desire.
At that time, he was like a noble sage who remains far removed from all evils and does not inflict harm upon others.

At a later time, he dwelt and roamed with a herd of deer by a river; its waters were vast and deep without bottom or shore, swollen by a violent torrent that swept away everything in its path, destroying mountain banks and uprooting great trees, such that no birds or beasts dared to approach.

At that time, there was a man who was being swept away by the water; terrified and trembling, he did not know where he was going. His physical strength grew faint and his remaining life was but a moment; raising his voice, he cried out loudly:
"O celestial deities and terrestrial spirits, who possesses compassion and can grant me rescue?"
Alas! Now I am parting from my family; today I am weary and distressed—upon whom can I rely?
I have heard in the past that there was once a deer in the world who practiced the dharma of the rishis and possessed great compassion; he alone would be able to see me deeply and deliver me.
At that time, the Deer King, hearing such a sound from before the herd of deer, looked around in alarm to see who was suffering distress, and spoke these words:
"Having heard this, my heart is pained; it is no different from their own suffering."
He then addressed the deer:
"You should all disperse as you please; I wish to seek out a level place where I may drink my fill of water to satisfy my thirst."
Upon hearing this, the deer immediately scattered in all four directions.
The Deer King then followed the sound to search for them, where he saw a man being swept away by the water, further struck by wood and stones, suffering great distress.
Upon seeing this, the Deer King immediately thought to himself:

"The current is so swift and violent that even a large fish could not cross it; now, my body is small and my strength is but slight—how can I possibly know whether I will be able to ferry this man across?"
"I would rather that my own body perish along with his; I truly cannot bear to see him suffer alone.
He further thought:

"If this man were on dry land and trapped by an elephant, I might be able to employ some skillful means to rescue and protect him. But now that he is adrift here in these turbulent waters, hurrying toward his end, how can I possibly deliver him?"
If I were to enter the water and fail to rescue them, everyone would hear of it and mock me, asking, "Knowing his own inability, why did he enter the water?
Although I now possess a heart of compassion, my physical strength is meager and I fear I cannot accomplish this task.
"I must now redouble my diligence and go to rescue them without ceasing.
He then spoke these words:
"You should not give rise to a heart of fear; as I now enter the water, I shall be like grass and wood; even if my body perishes, I must certainly save you."
At that time, the deer king leaped into the river and went to where the man was; he then commanded the drowning man to sit upon his back.

The drowning man sat down immediately, feeling secure and free from anxiety, as if a person were sitting comfortably on a couch or mat. However, the river abounded with wood and stones which struck against one another, causing the man’s body such excruciating pain that he could find no relief.
At that time, the deer king carried the drowning man on his back until death and would not let him go;
only then was the man able to reach the other shore. Having been rescued and safely emerged, the man then said to the deer king:
"The body that my parents nurtured has perished; this life and body now truly belong to you."
"Although you are a deer king, your life is now bound to mine; please grant me your command regarding what must be done.
At that time, the deer king said to the man: "Listen for a moment:
I do not seek any reward from you, nor do I harbor thoughts of pride. I do not begrudge such a life as this; I simply wish to bring benefit to others."

"You should now know that, though I have taken the body of a beast and constantly dwell in the forests and wilds, I roam at will seeking water and grass; although I do not encroach upon the villages and hamlets of human inhabitants."

However, I am burdened by many sins and numerous enemies and haters; furthermore, I am terrified of lions, tigers, wolves, and various predatory beasts, as well as hunters. I have no one to turn to for refuge and no one to protect me.

"Although my deer body is variegated and exquisite, no one in all the world has ever seen it; yet because you rescued me, you alone have seen it. In the past, I made a vow: 'If I see one in suffering or distress, I must deliver them. If a person possesses strength but fails to rescue another who sees their suffering, know that such a person shall receive no fruit or reward, just as one who does not sow seeds will not harvest a crop."
If you wish to honor me, you should carefully restrain your speech; one who recognizes and remembers kindness is praised by the noble and holy.
One who is ungrateful will have an evil reputation spread abroad in this present life, will be rebuked by the wise, and will undergo much suffering as an evil retribution in future lives.

One who knows gratitude finds peace and security in two worlds; they attain mastery not through the causes and conditions of material giving, and they possess great wisdom without needing to cultivate extensive learning. Though they lack bathing in water, they are pure and free from defilement; though they are apart from the scenting of perfumes, they obtain the unsurpassed fragrance; though they are without necklaces and ornaments, they achieve true adornment. Having distanced themselves from all dependencies, they attain self-protection; though they carry neither sword nor staff, no one will encroach upon them.

You should know this: the merit obtained by one who recognizes kindness is beyond description, and the faults incurred by one who fails to recognize it are likewise immeasurable; therefore, you must now carefully guard your speech.

At that time, having heard these words, the drowning man was filled with a mixture of grief and joy; his tears flowed profusely as he prostrated before the Deer-footed One and spoke thus: "You constantly preach the Dharma to all sentient beings, revealing the true path to Nirvana.

You are like a skilled physician who eradicates the suffering of the feverish diseases of the minds of sentient beings. You are the foremost compassionate father in the world; you are my honored guide. I truly desire to attend upon you, receiving your teachings morning and evening without wishing to be separated from you for even a single thought-moment; otherwise, I shall surely commit evil and be incapable of bearing [the consequences]."
"Even though I shall now depart and our physical forms will be separated, my heart does not yet dare to conceive the thought of abandoning you.
Having spoken these words, he immediately set out on his way.
The deer king looked back at him; once he was no longer visible in the distance, he returned to his original place among the herd of deer.

At that time, the man who had been rescued from drowning, having returned home, forgot the kindness shown to him and turned his back on righteousness. He destroyed the torch of the Dharma, allowing his own mind to go naturally to ruin; he felled the tree of the Dharma and planted a forest of poison. With his mind becoming a vessel for evil, filled with manifold resentments and poisons, he went to the king’s presence for the sake of immediate worldly profit and addressed the king, saying:

"Great King, you should know that recently I entered the mountains and saw a deer whose body color was as exquisite as a string of the seven precious gems, serving as the leader among the herd of deer."
"It is like the full moon amidst the host of stars; its hide is of variegated colors, fit for covering a carriage. Your Majesty, I know the place where this deer roams and dwells.
When the King heard this, his heart was filled with wonder and joy, and he said, "Show me the place, and I shall go there myself to capture it."
The drowning man replied to the king,
"I respectfully obey your command.
The king immediately prepared his carriage and ordered him to lead the way, while a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen followed in his wake.
At that time, the deer king was sleeping, utterly exhausted, amidst the herd of deer.
Then, many birds in the sky saw the king’s army and cavalry, and they said to one another:
"The king will surely come for the sake of the golden deer."
At that time, a crow immediately went to where the deer was and pecked at the ear of the deer king. Startled awake, the deer king thought to himself:

"For what reason has this crow come to awaken me? From time immemorial, when flocks of crows and their like have looked upon us or surrounded us, none dared to approach; why, then, does it violate my person today?"
The deer immediately rose up and gazed afar at the king’s army as it gathered from the four directions and drew near; he then thought again:
"These many crows are truly without fault. It is like a person whose honored one has fallen into a pit; if one pulls them out by the hand, how could that be a transgression?"
He further thought:

"These sentient beings lack a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; although lions, tigers, and wolves—the predators of this world—are my constant enemies, their hostile intent will immediately cease upon hearing me preach the Dharma."

This person is devoid of reason; having been born among humans, they have forgotten kindness and betrayed righteousness, turning against me to harbor malice. They are like a flower of exquisite fragrance placed upon a corpse—immediately loathsome and a sight no one wishes to behold.
"This person is just like that: for the sake of obtaining a small portion of happiness in the present life, they abandon the immeasurable rewards of happiness in the future.
At that time, the deer king spoke these words to the deer:
"Do not be distressed. The reason the king has come here now is solely for my sake, not for yours."

"Although I am now able to escape and flee to a distance, and though I could destroy and shatter his army, I must go to the king's presence myself, even at the cost of my life. If I do so, you shall all be scattered to the east and west, even unto the loss of your lives."
Therefore, for your sake, I shall now go to the king's presence; simply follow behind me and do not give way to fear, for I shall ensure that you all remain safe and free from harm.
"You should know this: if I were to resolve to enter nirvana, I could attain it immediately; yet the reason I do not take it is precisely for your sake.
Even if I must lose my life upon reaching the king's presence, provided that you are all brought to safety and fully delivered, I shall have no regrets."
Having spoken these words, he went at once to the king’s presence. Upon seeing him, the man who had been rescued pointed him out to the king, saying, "This is the very one you call the Deer King."
Having spoken these words, he let both hands fall to the ground.
When the king saw this, he immediately dismounted from his horse; his heart was struck with terror and his hair stood on end as he said:
"How is it that your hands have been severed and fallen off like this?"
He immediately cast aside his sword and staff and went alone to where the deer was.
When the deer saw the king, its heart was filled with distress. The king thought to himself:
"Though it has the body of a beast, it is no ordinary deer; it is the King of the Dharma who has emerged with valor."
At that time, the deer king addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, for what reason have you laid aside your sword and staff, with sweat flowing from your body as if you were terrified?
If it is because I have caused you fear, know this: I am one who has cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and shall never cause you harm; it is as impossible as the moon producing fire."
When the king heard this, his mind attained peace and security; he then turned toward the deer king and spoke these words:
"For what reason have these men fallen to the ground with both hands?"
However, as you said just now that you can grant us fearlessness,
how is it that this man directly showed you his body and received such a retribution?
You yourself just now said that you can grant all sentient beings freedom from fear.
"How can you cause this man to be thus?
If it is said that he did not give [the gift], then the entire world shall immediately burst into flames.
At that time, the deer king spoke again to the king, saying:

"For example, suppose there is a person who commits a grave offense against the state or offends a pure bhikṣu who dwells in non-contention; such a person incurs a great and heavy sin. One who is ungrateful incurs a great and heavy sin in exactly the same way."
"Your Majesty, you should now know that this person has acted of their own accord and shall receive the retribution for it themselves; it is not due to my causal conditions.
The King then asked:
"I pray you, explain this in detail; I wish to hear it."
The deer king replied, "I pray that Your Majesty question him; there is no need for me to speak.
The king then questioned the man:
"Why have you now caused both hands to fall to the ground?
At that time, the drowning man explained the original circumstances to the king in detail. Having heard this, the king said:
"Since you have committed such an act, how could you possibly avoid receiving retribution?"

If one is in distress and relies upon another, even for a single moment, one ought to repay that kindness; how much more so when one has received such profound favor over a long period? To fail to repay it and instead harbor malice and inflict harm—how could such a person not receive a corresponding retribution?

Just as a person, when weary from the heat, takes rest under a cool tree, that person ought not to damage even a single leaf of that tree; likewise, one who has received kindness should never forget it.
At that time, the king again addressed the deer king, kneeling with palms joined and speaking these words:
"From this day forward, I shall constantly take refuge in you."
The deer king replied,
"If this is truly so, I respectfully accept your intention.
The king spoke again:
"You have now accepted my request; what do you wish to seek?
The deer king replied, "If you can regard me with a sense of reverence, then listen attentively!"
"I am a beast; I rely solely on water and grass for my sustenance and seek nothing else.
Great King, you should know that in the past, when this man was adrift and distressed upon the water with no one to protect him and his life nearly at an end, I was still able to save him.
If Your Majesty now possesses a heart of compassion, you should regard this man as you would your own infant."

If one regards such a person, it is as if one regards me; this person is foolish and ignorant and is to be pitied. After their life ends, they will surely fall into hell, where for immeasurable years they will undergo all manner of suffering. Therefore, one should give rise to a heart of compassion toward such a person.
"Great King!
It is like a man who has many sons whom he loves equally, yet his heart is especially weighted toward one who is ill;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, for whom compassion and love are particularly directed toward evil sentient beings, because those beings harbor unwholesome dharmas."
"Therefore, the Bodhisattva arouses the mind of enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Great King again composed his countenance and spoke these words:

"You are now truly a Great Teacher who tames and guides; you are the protector and upholder of the True Dharma, the refuge for those in peril and distress, and one capable of removing all fears of sentient beings."
"These sentient beings have practiced many unwholesome dharmas and their bodies ought to sink into the earth; that they do not perish is surely due to the protection and support of the Great Being.

From this day forward, we grant the herd of deer the joy of fearlessness. We now vow to be your disciples for the rest of our lives, and if you attain the Unsurpassed Way in a future age, we pray that you will deliver us first."
