Thereupon, having spoken these words, the king immediately addressed his ministers:
"From this day forward, none of the people throughout the kingdom shall engage in hunting or killing as their livelihood."

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), although they may take the body of a beast, they do not give rise to even a single thought of malice toward their enemies or those who hate them.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas maintain their precepts even while dwelling in a state of anger,
how much more so when born among human beings— how could they fail to uphold them firmly?
As I have heard:
In the past, due to the causes and conditions of anger, the Bodhisattva fell among the dragons and received a body of the three poisons:
namely, the poison of breath, the poison of sight, and the poison of touch.

His body was of variegated colors like a heap of the seven treasures; its radiance illuminated itself without depending on the sun or moon, and his stature and appearance were grand, with a breath like the wind from a bellows.

His eyes shone brightly like two rising suns, and he was constantly surrounded by immeasurable nāgas, who transformed their own bodies into human forms to enjoy themselves together with him and the various nāga maidens.

He dwelt in a secluded place on Mount Vaidūrya, where the forests were vast and the flowers and fruits were so lush and abundant that it was most delightful; there were various ponds endowed with the eight excellent qualities of water, wherein he constantly stayed and enjoyed himself for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
At that time, for the sake of food and drink, the garuḍa soared through the air with its body coiled and came to seize them.
As it approached, the mountains were shattered and the springs and ponds dried up.

At that time, when the various nāgas and nāga maidens saw and heard these things, their hearts were filled with great terror; the necklaces, flower perfumes, and ornaments they wore immediately fell away and lay scattered upon the ground.
The nāga ladies were terrified and shed tears, saying:
"Now this great enemy has come to press upon us; his mouth is made of vajra and destroys everything—what shall we do?"
The nāga then replied, "You shall follow after me.
Thereupon, the women immediately went together to seek refuge with the nāga; the nāga then thought to himself:
"Now these women are each filled with terror; if I cannot provide protection for them, what is the use of such a magnificent body?
For the sake of all these dragon kings, if I cannot protect them, what is the use of being their king?"
Those who practice the True Dharma sacrifice their own bodies and lives to protect others; this King of the Garuḍas possesses great majesty and virtue.
His power is unbearable, and none except for my single person can resist it. I must now sacrifice my own body and life to save these nāgas.
At that time, the Dragon King said to the Garuḍa:
"You, O Garuḍa, deign to listen for a moment to what I shall say.

You have always harbored thoughts of enmity and harm toward me, yet I have never harbored a single thought of malice toward you. Because of my past karma, I have received this great body and am endowed with the three poisons; though I possess such power, I have never once conceived a thought of ill will toward another."

I now deliberate upon my own strength and find it sufficient to oppose you in combat; I can also cast myself into a great blazing fire or onto dry grass and wood; when the five grains are about to ripen, I can meet the calamity of a fierce hailstorm; I can transform my body into a vast size to obscure the sun and moon, or transform it into a minute size to enter the pores of a lotus fiber; I can also destroy the great earth to create rivers and seas, shake the mountain peaks until they tremble, or flee far away so that you cannot see me.
The reason I do not depart now is that many nāgas have come to rely upon me; the reason I do not engage you in battle is because I harbor no ill will toward you.
The garuḍa said:
"I am your enemy; why do you not harbor ill will toward me?
The nāga king replied:

"Though I am in the body of a beast, I well understand the retribution of karma; I know for certain that even for a small evil, retribution pursues one without ceasing, just as form and shadow do not part from one another.

The reason why I and you were both born into such an evil household is entirely due to the accumulation of evil karma in previous lives. I now constantly give rise to a heart of compassion toward you;
you should reflect deeply on what the Tathāgata has said: 'One cannot extinguish hatred through a hateful mind.'"
"Only through patience can one then extinguish it.
"It is like throwing dry firewood into a great fire; its flames increase even more than before. To repay anger with anger is just like this."
At that time, having heard these words, the garuḍa’s resentment immediately subsided, and he spoke thus to the nāga king:
"I have always harbored a heart of enmity toward you, yet you have instead conceived a heart of compassion for me."

The Dragon King replied, "I and you both received the Buddha’s words together in the past; I have always remembered and cherished them in my heart, whereas you have forgotten and failed to keep them in mind."
The garuḍa said:
"I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will become my preceptor and skillfully teach me the unsurpassed Dharma; from this day forward, I shall grant fearlessness to all the nāgas."
Having spoken these words, he immediately left the dragon palace and returned to his original dwelling place.
At that time, after the Dragon King had sent the garuḍa back to his own abode, he comforted the dragons and their women, saying:
"Did you see the garuḍa and feel fear?"
When other sentient beings behold you, they likewise give rise to great fear.
Just as you, O nāgas, cherish your own lives, so too do all sentient beings.

One should contemplate one's own body as being analogous to the bodies of others; therefore, one should give rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). By virtue of the causes and conditions accumulated through my cultivation of this compassionate mind, may those who harbor enmity and hatred return to their original place. Among all things that can be relied upon within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), none surpasses the compassionate mind.
Compassion is the sublime medicine that removes heavy afflictions; compassion is the sublime food for those starving amidst the immeasurable cycle of birth and death.

Because we lost our compassionate mind in the past, we have now fallen into this state among animals. If one takes the cultivation of compassion as the gateway, no afflictions can enter; it leads to rebirth among gods and humans, as well as to true liberation. Compassion is the excellent vehicle, and there is nothing superior to it.
When the female nāgas heard these words, they abandoned their poisonous malice and cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
At that time, the nāga king saw his own kind all cultivating a mind of loving-kindness; filled with joy and self-congratulation, he exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"What I have now accomplished is already done; though I was born among the animals due to my karmic causes, I have been able to practice the deeds of a Great Being.
At that time, the Dragon King again addressed the dragons, saying:

"I have finished performing good deeds for you, and I have shown you the true and correct Way. Furthermore, I have lit the torch of the True Dharma for you, closed off all evil paths, and opened the road to the human and celestial realms. You have cast away immeasurable poisonous evils and taken the supreme nectar in their place. Now, I wish to request one thing of you."

"You should know that on the fifteenth day before the twelfth month, the people of Jambudvīpa bathe their bodies with the water of the eight precepts and purify their minds, making this a provision for the realms of humans and devas. They remain far removed from pride, arrogance, greed, anger, and delusion; I shall do likewise, wishing to emulate those people by receiving the dharma of the eightfold fast."

You should know this: if one can receive and uphold these eight precepts, though lacking fine garments, one is able to bathe; though lacking walls, one is able to ward off enemies and thieves; though lacking parents, one possesses a noble lineage; without various necklaces and ornaments, the body is naturally adorned; though lacking precious jewels, one possesses immeasurable great wealth; and though lacking carriages and horses, it is called the Mahāyāna. Without relying on bridges or ferries, one crosses over the evil realms. Such are the merits of one who receives the eight precepts.
"You should now know that I always uphold it in every place.
The nāgas each asked,
"What is called the Dharma of the Eight Precepts and Fasting?"
The Dragon King replied:
"As for the eight precepts of the fast:
the first is not to kill;..."
Second, not to steal;
third, not to engage in sexual misconduct;
fourth, not to speak falsely.
Fifth, not drinking alcohol;
sixth, not sitting or lying on high or wide beds;
seventh, not wearing fragrant flowers or necklaces, nor anointing the body with perfumes.
Eighth, one does not engage in singing, dancing, or music, nor does one go to watch or listen to them;
these eight matters constitute the adornment of not eating past midday. This is called the Dharma of the Eight Precepts and Fasting (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).

The nāgas asked, “If we were to be separated from the King for even a short time, our lives could not be sustained. Now, wishing to cause the unsurpassed True Dharma to flourish and to keep the lamp of the Dharma blazing, we request to receive your command.”
The benefits of the Buddha-dharma are applicable everywhere; why, then, should one not receive and uphold it within this very context?

We have also heard that there are laypeople who are able to cultivate wholesome dharmas; if one practices wholesome dharmas while at home, they likewise increase—why must one necessarily seek a secluded place?
The Dragon King replied:
"In the realm of desire, the mind for sensual pleasures does not pause even for a moment; upon seeing exquisite forms, one gives rise to the desires of the past.
It is just as rain easily turns a damp ground into mud; likewise, upon seeing exquisite forms, one gives rise to the desires of the past."
"If one dwells in deep mountains, one does not see forms; if one does not see forms, the mind of desire does not arise.
The nāgas asked:
"If one stays in deep mountains, one’s [virtue] will increase; you who uphold the True Dharma may go wherever you wish."
At that time, the Dragon King immediately led the dragons to a secluded place, far removed from thoughts of lust and anger.
He further cultivated great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, adorned himself with the perfection of patience, and opened the path to Bodhi.
Having undertaken the eight precepts for himself and maintained the pure fast for many days, his body grew weak from fasting; he was overcome by extreme hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and sleep.
The Dragon King practiced these eight precepts and was fully endowed with patience, harboring no thought of harm toward any sentient being.
At that time, an evil person arrived at the dragon’s dwelling; while the dragon was fast asleep, he heard the sound of footsteps and immediately woke up in alarm.
At that time, when the wicked men saw this, their hearts were filled with wonder and joy, and they said to one another,
"What mass of jewels has emerged from the earth?
When the dragon saw the thoughts arising in the minds of these men, he immediately conceived a thought:

"I have come to this place to cultivate virtue, yet within these mountains there are those who are wicked and rebellious, who destroy the cultivation of virtue. If they were to see my true form, they would die of terror; once they have died of terror, I would then be unable to practice the True Dharma."
"In the past, due to the causes and conditions of anger, I received this dragon body; it is fully possessed of the three poisons, with venom in my breath, my sight, and my touch.
Now that these people have come here, they will surely covet my body and cut short my life."
Then, those wicked men said to one another again:

"We have entered the mountains for many years seeking wealth and profit, yet we have never before seen such a dragon’s body, adorned with such brilliant patterns that it delights the eye. If we were to flay its skin and present it to our king, we would surely receive a heavy reward."
At that time, the wicked men immediately used sharp knives to flay his skin.

The Dragon King, whose mind at all times seeks the benefit and happiness of the entire world, conceived thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward these people; because he practiced this loving-kindness, the three poisons were instantly extinguished.
Furthermore, he exhorted and comforted his own mind, saying:
"You should not now cherish or begrudge this body; though you wish to protect it for many years, when the time arrives, it cannot be avoided."
"These people, out of greed for my reward, will now fall into hell because of me; it would be better for me to die myself than to cause them to suffer in this very life."
The men immediately stepped forward, seized their knives, and began to flay him; the dragon then reflected:
"If a person is without fault and someone dismembers them, yet they accept it silently without retaliation and harbor no resentment, one should know that such a person is a great and upright being."
If one maintains silent endurance toward parents, siblings, wives, or children, this is not worthy of praise.
If one develops a mind of silent acceptance toward enemies, this alone is truly noble.
Therefore, for the sake of sentient beings, I should now endure this in silence; if I can maintain such endurance toward them, they shall truly become my companions and my spiritual friends.

Therefore, I should now conceive the thought of this person as my father or mother; for although I have sacrificed my body and life throughout immeasurable past eons, I have never before been able to do so for even a single sentient being.

If that person thinks, "Once this skin has been peeled off, I shall obtain immeasurable precious treasures and valuable goods," may I, in future lives, always grant such a person immeasurable Dharma-wealth.
At that time, having been flayed, the dragon king’s entire body bled; the pain was unbearable, and his whole body trembled so violently that he could not support himself.
Then, countless small insects, smelling the scent of his blood, all gathered there to devour his flesh. The dragon king thought again:
"May these small insects who eat my body be granted the food of the Dharma in a future life."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they do not give rise to resentment even when their skin is flayed and their flesh eaten; how much less so in other circumstances?
